speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be repetitious. I hope that anything I say today with reference to the Budget Speech the Minister delivered yesterday will be new and fresh.
I want to start by adverting to the situation with respect to unemployment. Probably the most serious deficiency in the Budget is that it does not provide for any long-term recovery in Canada. That, of course, is because it does not show any way in which we are going to get out of the Government's existing deficit position in the next five years. It does not show any way in which we are going to achieve lower real interest rates or lower interest rates in the next five years. It does not show how the present economic recovery is going to continue successfully.
It is also noticeable because of the apparent inability of the Government to deal with the question of unemployment, the
1,473,000	Canadians who are now unemployed. The document that gives the figures for the fiscal plan is astonishing. When
you get behind the figures and the phraseology in his Budget, it shows that the Minister is contemplating that this year there will be 1,401,000 Canadians unemployed on average during the year. In 1984-85 he contemplates 1,336,000 Canadians will remain unemployed. In 1985-86 he is contemplating
1,238,000	Canadians remaining unemployed all year. In 198687 there will be 1,184,000 people unemployed, the Minister prophesied. In 1987-88, even then, 1,106,000 Canadians are to remain unemployed if this Government remains in office.
I can only tell you, Mr. Speaker, that we do not intend to contemplate those kinds of unemployment figures for Canada when we assume power whenever this Government calls an election. These figures are not good enough. That is why the Minister's Budget appears on the surface to have something to it; but when one looks underneath, as I said last night, it reminds me of a capelin, a little fish that rolls in on the beaches in Newfoundland having his last jolly spasm on the way. The capelin lies on the beach in Newfoundland in the moonlight for a few days. It looks bright and shiny on the surface but once you give it a poke, you find it is completely rotten inside. That is the trouble with this Budget. It is shiny on the surface but completely deteriorated on the inside. That is the Minister's projection of unemployment for Canadians in the next five years.
We hear the Minister in this House tell us how much better we are doing than the rest of the world, how proud he is of our recovery, and how much better off we are than the United States. The unemployment rate in the United States is now 8 per cent. Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, that in 1968 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) formed his administration the unemployed rate was 4.8 per cent? There were 360,000 people unemployed. That is a great record. If the Prime Minister stays in power long enough, there will be no Canadians employed. There was 4.5 per cent unemployment when the Prime Minister assumed office in 1968.
Let us look at what it was in March, 1980 when the "terrible Tories" left power. By the way, that was the only year the deficit had been reduced in a number of years. In the eight months we were in power, what was the situation? In March, 1980 the unemployment rate was 7.5 per cent. There were 967,000 people unemployed in the winter of 1980. Four years later there are 1,473,000 Canadians unemployed and we have a government that contemplates some remaining unemployed for the rest of the 1980s. If it is not time for that Government, that tired, dispirited group of montebanks to leave office, then when will the time come? Will anyone be left employed if this Government continues in office? There were

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
360,000	Canadians unemployed when Mr. Trudeau was elected Prime Minister and today we have 1,473,000 Canadians unemployed.
There is another point I want to make in connection with the Government's figures that have been presented to the House. These are five-year projections. The Government has projected, of course, horrendous deficits, as I mentioned yesterday, totalling $142.1 billion over the next five years. It is a fantastic series of deficits, and there are fantastic increases in spending. Are even those projections accurate?
The Government projects $114 million in interest payments alone and $119 million to be borrowed. Are those figures accurate? As you know, Mr. Speaker, we do not know what interest rate calculations the Government is using. We do know from looking at what the Government says the expenditures will be that the Government is using some peculiar figures. For example, the Government says total outlays this year-expenditures-will be $90,076 billion; the year after they will be $99.3 billion; the following years $108.5 billion; $118.4 billion and $128.3 billion. That is what the Government tells us.
[DOT] (MI5)
These are the increases in percentage terms: 7.6 per cent this year; in 1985, 5.3 per cent; in 1986, 5.6 per cent and in 1987, 6.0 per cent. That is the percentage increase in expenditures each year.
Then they show that the cost of living in those years will go up. In 1984 the figure is 5.2 per cent; 1985, 5.3 per cent; 1986, 4.8 per cent and in 1987, 4.5 per cent. They show that during the same years the Gross National Product will go up. In 1984 it will go up by 10.3 per cent; 1985, 9.3 per cent; 1986, 9.1 per cent; and 1987, 8.3 per cent.
Let us compare the percentage increases in the Government's expenditures or what it tells us they are going to increase by each year. We see, for example, that in 1985 the Government says its expenditures will go up 5.3 per cent and the cost of living will go up by exactly the same. We know that there is practically no chance whatsoever that these are accurate projections of the expenditure increases. We therefore know that under this regime the deficits will be even more horrendous.
When we see that in 1985 the GNP goes up by 9.3 per cent and Government spending only goes up by 5.3 per cent, we know that there is a large measure of fiction in the figures that the Minister is asking us to believe are estimates.
That brings me to another point, Mr. Speaker. What is the Government's record for the accuracy of what it tells the House and the people of Canada is going to be the situation from year to year? I hope this will not bore hon. gentlemen because it will take a few minutes.
By the way, I have some quotations. In 1969-70 the Prime Minister said on August 13 that we would be on the road to financial disaster if nothing was done to bring spending under control. That was what the Prime Minister said in 1969-70,
Mr. Speaker. That year we spent $13.8 billion. That was the total spending of the Government when the poor Prime Minister said we would be on the road to financial disaster if nothing was done to control spending. We had a surplus that year of $493 million and our net debt was $18.1 billion. The Prime Minister was worried about the road to financial disaster then, 14 years ago.
This may be of interest, Mr. Speaker. On May 6, 1972 Mr. John Turner said:
The bare fact of the matter is that we cannot do everything at once. We simply don't have the resources. There are limits to the scope of fiscal policy. There are limits to stimulus and readjustment.
He had spending of $20.8 billion and the net debt was $18.8 billion. That gentleman may have a resurrection this year if the Prime Minister is not resurrected for the second time. If he does not beat the record set several thousand years ago, then it may be that Mr. Turner will have a resurrection. On November 19, 1974 he said:
We must do all we can in these circumstances to restrain the growth of government expenditures .. . We have sought and shall continue to seek to cut out public waste, to place limits on the growth of the public service, and to approve only the most essential new programs.
That was the policy of the Government in 1974-75. The total spending was $30.8 billion, the deficit was $1.7 billion and the net debt was $21.1 billion.
The next year, on June 23, 1975, in his Budget address, Mr. Turner said:
The Government proposes to set an example of restraint in this regard by imposing strict control over its activities and programs.
Have you ever heard such a list of protestations of restraint and control, Mr. Speaker? He spent $36.5 billion, had a deficit of $5.4 billion and a net debt of $22.9 billion. Along came Mr. Donald Macdonald, now the Chairman of a Royal Commission that is pointing out our economic future. On May 25, 1977 he said:
To achieve our expenditure central objectives, the introduction of new programs must be kept within careful limits, and the resources required for the continued operation of existing programs must be minimized ... It is appropriate that these record deficits should recede.
That was the pious hope of Mr. Donald Macdonald, now the guiding genius of the Macdonald Royal Commission. He spent $40.3 billion, his deficit was $6.2 billion and the net debt $28.3 billion. He had a Budget the next year as well. On March 31, 1977 he said:
The restraint of growth in the government's spending has been an integral of our anti-inflation policies. The Government believes that such restraint is as important today as it was at the start of the program.
He had a $45.5 billion expenditure, $10.8 billion deficit and a $34.6 billion net public debt. The Liberals are restraining themselves so much, Mr. Speaker, they are suffering from hernia in the Liberal caucus.
In 1978-79, the new Minister of Finance, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), now out on the campaign trail, said on November 16: "There can be no
February 16, 1984

weakening in our determination to keep expenditures under tight control". What did he spend? He spent $49.3 billion. What was his deficit? His deficit was $12.2 billion. What was the net debt at the start of the fiscal year? It was $44.8 billion.
In 1979-80, we have the Prime Minister interested in the game now, nine or 10 years later. He has become alarmed about what he said in 1970. I believe he went on TV. He had a dramatic conversion on the road on one of his trips. He has had more trips than Bob Hope and Bing Crosby put together. That is the most travelled family, Mr. Speaker, since the Love Boat. On January 12, 1980, during the election campaign, the Prime Minister said:
We will hold the line on government expenditure growth to under the rate of GNP . . . The deficit will be reduced in a phased and orderly fashion ... Any new expenditure programs to meet the evolving needs and requirements of Canadians will be financed by reallocating existing expenditures or by increases in revenues. We will not add to the deficit by adding new programs.
What did Government spend that year? It spent $54.4 billion. The deficit was $11.4 billion, reduced from the previous year. Why? Because the Conservatives had slipped into office for eight months and then slipped out again, and brought the deficit under control. What was the net debt at the start of the year? It was $57.1 billion.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, had I continued on as Minister of Finance, we would not today be looking at 1,473,000 unemployed Canadians. There would be hundreds of thousands fewer.
We can see, Mr. Speaker, that this is a Government fantastically interested in restraint and control of expenditures, one horrified and shocked by deficits and determined to crush the deficit, because that is their rhetoric every year.
In 1980-81, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) said in one of his great Budgets on October 20, 1980:
In order to achieve the essential reduction in the deficit, great restraint over expenditures has, therefore, been required.
But not in Cape Breton. The Celtic sphinx was not restraining things down in Cape Breton. He spent $62.8 billion. He had a deficit of $12.6 billion. The net debt was $68.5 billion. He had a deficit of $12.6 billion. The net debt was $68.5 billion.
He brought in another Budget for 1981-82. The November 12 Budget had three themes; restraint, equity and economic renewal. He said:
For our part, I believe we must reduce our deficit and our borrowing requirements substantially.
What did he do, apart from what he said? He spent $75 billion. He had a deficit of $13.6 billion. The net debt was $81.2 billion. "But he said, "We must reduce our deficit and our borrowing requirements substantially".
Then he brought in another budget on June 28, 1982, in which he said:
Some say it (the Government) should print more money.
They certainly do, and he is one of the biggest ones.
Others say it should let the deficit rip.
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
Oh, it would never do that.
But that would fail miserably.
Well, if letting the deficit "rip" would fail miserably, why has it let the deficit rip?
Inflation and unemployment would get worse.
The Minister of Finance knew what was going to happen if they let the deficit rip; inflation and unemployment would get worse. But he let it rip. He did not have a seat left in his pants, it ripped so much.

Then he went on to say interest rates would rise even more. The former Minister of Finance is prophesying exactly what happened. Then he said Canada would price itself out of world markets and recovery would be postponed. That is what the then Minister of Finance said June 28, 1982. He said if we let the deficit rip, inflation and unemployment will get worse, interest rates will rise even more, we will price ourselves out of world markets and recovery will be postponed. What does he do? He lets the deficit rip. Spending was $89.5 billion, the deficit $25.2 billion. The previous year's deficit was $13 billion.
The Deputy Prime Minister was not going to let the deficit rip; he was going to keep her under tight control and she doubled. Doubled! Everything he said would happen that was wrong if he let that happen, happened. Yet the Liberals are continuing to govern. They have been there for years; they are going to brazen it out and cling on for another few months in light of that record.
What about the next year? Why, the next year we had the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on April 19, 1983 say: "This is a fiscally responsible Budget". Well, this is indeed good news. It is the first fiscally responsible Budget we have seen from this crew. What does he do? He spends $100.2 billion. He has a deficit of $31.3 billion, of which $200 million was caused by his Budget leaking; the only Canadian Minister of Finance ever caught in the act of leaking. The deficit turns out not to be $31.3 billion, it is $31.5 billion. What was the net debt of this country at the start of the year? It was $119.2 billion. What does he now tell us our net debt is going to be at the end of March, 1984? Our net debt is going to be $150.9 billion, some 38.8 per cent of the GNP, the highest it has been as a percentage of the GNP since 1951 or so, which resulted from the war years. The average per capita debt is $6,011, the highest ever in our history. That is where this fiscally responsible Budget, this fiscally responsible Minister-all of those Ministers-are leaving us. Every one of them, every year, has fought the good fight against the deficit.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, the present Minister of Finance is a spritely dancer, as you will see from The Globe and Mail. He is the Jimmy Durante of Canadian Ministers of Finance. Old "Schnozz" himself.

The Budget-Mr. Crosbie

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
But this is a Government that can make the most Christian among us feel positively negative. Just let me refer again to the same problem. The previous Minister of Finance is now the Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs, and never has a Minister been able to obscure and obfuscate our external policy such as this Minister has. Luckily the Prime Minister has taken a great interest in foreign affairs so the Deputy Prime Minister is not needed to put his nose into affairs that are more foreign to him than anyone else. On October 28, 1980, that former Minister of Finance promised that over the fiscal period of 1983-84 there would be a steady reduction in the Government's deficit and financial requirements.
Now I am coming to the point of how accurate estimates are. He said only a moderate reduction in the deficit was needed in the next year. Of course, it went up. He said he expected the budgetary deficit to decline from $14.2 billion in 1980 to $13.7 billion in 1981-82, and then more sharply to $12.1 billion in 1982-83, and to $11.8 billion in 1983-84. The Minister was bravely projecting what the deficit was going to be for the next three years. Let us see how successful he and all of those people who work for him in the fortress of Finance were. He forecast the deficit for 1982-83 would be $12.1 billion. In fact, it was $24.6 billion. This Minister asks us to believe that his projections for the next five years, which are horrendous, are accurate when his predecessor's forecast of a deficit for 1982-83 of $12.1 billion was doubled. He forecast the deficit of 1983-84 at $11.8 billion. That is the year ending at the end of March. The Deputy Prime Minister said the deficit would be $11.8 billion. It is $31.5 billion. That is three times, Mr. Speaker. Three eights are twenty-four, three ones are three and three ones are three! I, at least, am careful mathematically. It is almost three times that the Minister estimated it would be. If the same mistakes are being made by this Minister, it leads us to deficits of $70 billion and $75 billion as opposed to $25 billion and $26 billion. If this Minister is as accurate as the other Minister, that is what we are let to. There is no reason to believe that this Minister is any more accurate than the other Minister. They are both "bass ackward".
In his Budget of November 12 the Minister said:
I believe we must reduce our deficit and our borrowing requirements substantially-even more than I proposed a year ago. This will take pressures off credit markets, ease interest rates and provide room for needy borrowers.
That is when the Government was borrowing $10 billion or $11 billion a year. He wanted to take the pressure off the credit markets, ease interest rates and provide room for needy borrowers. This Minister says we do not need to worry about borrowing $27 billion from the financial markets. He says we do not need to take pressure off the credit markets. This Minister says we do not need to ease interest rates or provide room for needy borrowers because he has been so successful they do not want to borrow. Our economy is so bustling and hustling that no one wants to borrow but the Government. That is the great record of success that this Minister has had.
The Deputy Prime Minister said; "I have set myself the task of cutting back the deficit in the next two fiscal years". I have shown you how successful he was in that task. In his final Budget of June 28, 1982 the Deputy Prime Minister said: "The Government cannot responsibly add to the deficit". That is what he said; but the Government has tripled the deficit. It used to be thought that a Minister of Finance had to be truthful, honest, scrupulous, careful in his statements, careful not to exaggerate and not to frighten the financial markets, rather than people who would say the Government cannot responsibly add to the deficit and then double and triple the deficit. Is it any wonder there is a lack of confidence in the country? Is it any wonder that people from outside Canada do not want to invest in Canada and that Canadians are moving their money out to the U.S. and elsewhere? Zanzibar, Afghanistan or any other country looks better than investing in Canada. We cannot believe a word our Ministers of Finance say.
There can be no confidence in this kind of chicanery and inaccuracy, Mr. Speaker. The Government does not only have budgets, it has economic statements. When the Government wants to pretend matters are not as serious, it has an economic statement. The Minister said the Budget deficit for 1982-83 would be $23.6 billion. That was when the financial year was half over. It was actually $24.6 billion. He put before us the biggest borrowing Bill the Government ever asked the House to grant it, claiming the deficit for the year would be $27.2 billion. The deficit for the year was not $27.2 billion, it was $24.6 billion. In other words, you cannot believe a word these Ministers say, Mr. Speaker. We know what has happened through the 10 or 12 years I have given you the quotations for. That is why this country can only be described as being in a sad state.
A few weeks ago the Minister called for a social contract with the Canadian people. He wants a social contract. The contract the Canadian people want is the contract they now have out on the Government. That is the only contract they want with the Government.
The political process, Mr. Speaker, has been so prostituted for political purposes by the Liberal Party now in power that
February 16, 1984

when you pay taxes today you should get recognition for a deductible contribution to the Liberal Party because the money is not being used for public purposes. Wherever possible, it is being diverted to partisan political purposes such as we have seen in the Prime Minister's Office in recent days.
What is the fastest growing thing in Canada today, Mr. Speaker? It is not worry and fear in the Liberal caucus and it is not projects in Liberal ridings. It is the debt servicing cost of the Government of Canada. Apart from all other concerns with the debt, the average term to maturity of Government debt today has fallen to five and one-quarter years from six and one-half. In other words, all this indebtedness of the Government now has an average term of only five and one-quarter years. The Government has to repay it all within five and one-quarter years. This includes Canada Savings Bonds of $90 billion. About two-thirds of all this debt matures in three years or less. Two-thirds of this tremendous amount of debt matures and has to be refinanced in the next three years. Let that give you pause.
The Auditor General himself has said that these figures are not accurate and do not show properly what the debt is. The Auditor General pointed out that the debt last year was understated by $5.3 billion. Even the fantastic figure shown last year was understated by $5.3 billion because unemployment insurance transactions of $3.28 billion are not shown. The Government has nothing in the books to show the losses of Canadair of over $1 billion and the losses of de Haviiland and the like.
Last year the Government did an exercise to show how much of the deficit was structural and how much was cyclical to try to help explain why the debt was so large. Unfortunately, its studies last year and this year show that of the present debt over half is structural. Even with a booming economy we would still have a deficit this year of $18 billion. The more you look at what is happening, the worse it appears.
In his Budget the Minister tries to pretend that we are going to have great growth this year. Other independent agencies such as the Conference Board of Canada, which has a much better record than the Government, predicts 3.3 per cent and .3 per cent for next year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Look at the OECD.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Every time I look at the OECD I see how badly Canada compares to the rest of the OECD and I get depressed. That is why I do not want to look at the OECD.
In February, 1983 Statistics Canada said the value of goods and services declined .2 per cent. On January 31 Statistics Canada said softness of investment plans in Canada contrast with strong gains in the U.S. What is there is this Budget that will make investment plans stronger rather than softer? There is nothing. There is not anything in this Budget that will attract anyone to invest here in Canada. Our industrial capacity which is utilized at.the present time I believe is 70 per cent. It is Statistics Canada itself that is giving the lie to what the Minister says, that softness of investment plans in Canada contrast with strong gains in the U.S.
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
How scrupulous is the Government to assist Canadian consumers and taxpayers? I mentioned the Canadian ownership charge yesterday. The Government has taken that, without the consent or authority of the House, and instead of leaving these funds in a special fund, has put it in general revenue to reduce its deficit. Yet the deficit still becomes $31.5 billion.
What was it the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said on November 22, 1983? I could not find the quote from the Toronto Star last night but he said: "The tax stays but we are still studying what to do with the money". How is that for arrogance? The Government now taxes the Canadian people before it even knows what it wants to do with the money. If that is not the epitome of arrogance. "The tax stays", says the Minister while beating his chest-because he is like a gorilla running across the country-"because I say the tax stays, and to heck with the Canadian consumer. We are still studying what to do with the money". Now we know what he is doing with the money. He is using it just to try to keep the deficit down to $31.5 billion.
While we are looking at the truthfulness of the Government, what did the Deputy Prime Minister say about the Canadian ownership charge when it was imposed on October 28, 1980? At page 11 of that speech he promised the Canadian people that:
Revenue for the Account will be provided by a Canadian ownership charge imposed on all oil and gas consumption in Canada which will come into operation as the acquisition program progresses and will be set at a level to ensure that the program will be totally self-financing, and in no way affect the government's deficit.
That was the solemn promise made on October 28, 1980, when the Canadian public were taxed one cent per litre on heating oil, gasoline and every product made from a barrel of oil. It is 4.5 cents a gallon; $840 million this year; $960 billion next year and $1 billion that it will take the year after. We were told that the program would be self-financing and in no way affect the Government's deficit. What does the Government do four years later? It reduces the deficit by $800 million or $420 million for this year, I believe, because it has taken $500 million to use for Dome-if Dome ever needs the $500 million, because Dome has taken the Government for far more than $500 million. Now it is used to affect the Government's deficit. Can one believe a word that such a motley crew as this enunciates? Of course one cannot. One hates to have to say it.
Just in passing, as a person who comes from the Atlantic provinces, what a disgraceful belabouring they have been given in the Atlantic provinces in the last three or four years. The Government has dismantled DREE. It did away with DREE in January, 1981 and we will now have what the Government calls ERDAs. It did away with DREE, replaced it with DRIE and we will now have ERDAs, Economic Regional Development Agreements.
The money spent in Newfoundland by DREE has decreased by something like 70 per cent of 80 per cent in the last several years. I understand that the Government will spent $2 billion in ERDAs of which $1.2 billion goes to Quebec and $30

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Crosbie
million, for example, to Alberta. That is called equity by the Government; $1.2 billion in Quebec and $30 million in Alberta. I do not know if it will spend anything in Newfoundland.
That is what has happened to the great program to overcome regional disparity. Do Members recall the Prime Minister in 1968 when he was on the diving boards of the country? His great theme was that he was going to overcome regional disparity. This is what has happened to his attempt to overcome regional disparity.
The present Minister of Finance said on September 15: "The top economic priority is the creation of jobs to ease our serious unemployment". Where does that appear in this Budget? What happened to that priority of September 15? On January 23, when he spoke to the Canadian Club in Toronto- memories are so short-he said:
Budgetary policies in 1984 must also respect the need for stability in the economic and fiscal environment. That means holding firm to the fiscal policy track-
He has his fiscal policy track suit on.
-on which the deficit will be restrained and then reduced as the recovery strengthens.
That is what he said to the Canadian Club on January 23 of this year. What has happened to that proposal? What is the point of the Minister making speeches if he will not carry out what he says in those speeches?
The Government said in the 1983 Throne Speech:
A comprehensive program will be presented to encourage economic growth so that more Canadians can own a home, learn a trade, expand a business, participate in the ownership of our resources, and gain a fair share of the abundant benefits this country can provide.
Where is the comprehensive program? This is the Government's Budget for 1984 and there is no such program. I mentioned yesterday that the Minister of Finance's dominant concern last April was to help 1.5 million Canadians who want to work but cannot find jobs. He has done nothing for them. In the Budget of last April the Minister said:
I expect strong growth to continue through 1984 at an average rate of 5.2 per cent. It will also become more broadly based as investment gathers strength.
Neither of those expectations has been fulfilled. The recovery is not broadly based.
I mentioned what Statistics Canada has reported. It said:
The narrowing of sources of growth in domestic demand is also reflected in the regional distribution of economic activity... In fact, Central Canada has accounted for all of the increase in employment since June as net declines have since been registered in Western Canada, notably Alberta and British Columbia.
Where is the broad-based growth that the Minister said would occur just 10 months ago? How does the Budget address the fact that the broad-based recovery promised in April has not occurred? Where can we point to in the Budget to show how the broad-based recovery is going to be achieved?
The special recovery tax imposed last April will cost Canadians $805 million this financial year. It will cost $2.4 billion in 1985-86 and $2,975 billion in 1986-87. The Minister calls it the special recovery tax. He should rename it the special recession tax. There is no recovery. This tax is not
going to help it, this special recession tax. Again, Statistics Canada said on January 31:
The economic recovery appeared to lose some of its vitality in the fourth quarter, and it is likely that this slow-down will continue early in 1984. The moderation of growth has been most evident in domestic demand.
Where does the Minister help domestic demand in this Budget? He does not help it at all because he increases taxes and takes four times the revenue he has given back in the various matters he mentioned yesterday. He might help demand if he did away with the Canadian ownership tax. He would help consumer demand if he did away with the 1 per cent increase in the federal sales tax that is coming in October. It is a regressive tax that bears more heavily on lower income people.
The Minister brings in pension changes that favour the wealthy, increasing the RRSP limit as he has. Where in this Budget does he help to increase domestic demand? If anyone on the other side can point to where he does that, then we will pleased to listen.
The increase in sales tax in October will cost Canadians $365 million. That is for this financial year. Of course, it will be a much greater amount next year when it has been in effect for a full year.
What is the main problem or obstacle to continued economic recovery? We can look to the Conference Board or other economic specialists. I would like to quote the Conference Board where it said: "Interest rates, given the rate of inflation, remain high and thus are unable to provide the usual stimulus to economic activity as would be the case in normal cyclical recoveries". What has this Budget done to address that question? Nothing. The Budget papers indicate in two places that the Government expects interest rates to decline, but the Government refuses to tell us what interest rate projections they are using in calculating debt repayment costs for the next five years.
The current Bank of Canada rate is 10 per cent. It is higher than it was last April. Is that a sign that interest rates will go down? The prime rate of the Bank is 11 per cent. Inflation has dropped significantly during that period, but it has not affected interest rates. Why not? It is because no one with money to invest trusts this Government. They know the Government is incapable of operating the economic affairs of the country. They know that if this Government continues in power, we will have renewed inflation and economic disaster. That is why they will not lower their interest rates now. As I said last night, the Budget has done nothing to bring about lower interest rates, to increase consumer demand or business investment, which are the three essentials if we are to have a real economic recovery.
It is a sorry story. By the way, when Liberal Members have a chance to speak in this debate, I hope they will not be tiresome and keep referring to some alleged article in The Globe and Mail of Toronto by "yours truly", unless they are going to look at it more accurately. I was honest enough to say
February 16, 1984

that the Budget of last April contained a proper general approach. That was the right kind of general approach compared with the disasters of his predecessors. The general approach was right, but that general approach has disappeared, and now the Minister has joined his predecessor in the march to inexorable disaster. This Budget guarantees Canadians a dubious and diminishing economic future. He has joined the march. He has arrested nothing, and he no longer moves in a direction that is satisfactory. He now has no chance of bringing economic recovery to Canada.
Of course, we will have other speakers in this debate who will be tackling different phases of the Budget-the question of pension reform, which is important; improvements in the assessment practices of the Department of National Revenue, which we forced the Government to commence and bring about. That is important as well. These things will all be discussed.
In this connection, I want to move the following amendment to the Budget:
That all the words following the word "That" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this House regrets the failure of the Government to present measures designed to reduce Canada's budgetary deficit, lower existing high interest rates, reduce crippling high levels of unemployment or to create meaningful pension reform all of which are needed as a result of years of government economic mismanagement and condemns the Government for its continued misuse of public funds and arrogant maladministration which have led to a crisis in public trust and confidence in government".
To top off this record I have given this morning, this resume of economic mismanagement, wrong estimating, deceit of the public, complete lack of control or fidelity-as though that were not bad enough-there is not anyone in the country with an ounce of impartiality who does not look at Ottawa and see a government which is wallowing in the worst kind of stable politics. I mean "stable" in the sense of a stable in which one keeps animals. They see leading this country a group of people who are prepared to do anything to keep themselves in power. That destroys confidence. The only hope the country has is that before too long there will be an election and we will have an opportunity to give the people of Canada an alternative and to show what we can do with the economic administration of this country. That is the only hope. Even if this group brought into the House a set of perfect policies to fit our economic circumstances, they would be unsuccessful as they cannot work without confidence. And there is no confidence in this Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to rise today to respond on behalf of the New Democratic Party to the Budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) yesterday and try to find some way to visualize what kind of a Budget it was. Over the last number of hours we have had responses as different groups indicated their reaction to the Budget.
I want you to imagine for a moment the Minister of Finance in a worn, torn, old suit to which he has sewn brightly coloured and brightly covered sequins. When he walked into the House of Commons yesterday to deliver his speech, the floodlights gave a glimmering appearance to this man on stage. Actually he looked kind of good with his glimmering sequins on his suit. A few hours later, taking advantage of the sunshine of the next day, the real worn and torn fabric of that suit comes through.
So be it with this particular Budget. Last night when people heard the Budget, there were feelings that there were some
good aspects to the Budget, that there was something for everyone. When you analyze carefully item by item what was in the Budget, you find that indeed there were some things in that Budget that will make people very happy, particularly a very select and special, elite group in Canadian society.
One document which the Minister of Finance gave out as part of his Budget is entitled: "The Canadian Economy in Recovery". I suspect that most Canadians over the last number of months have not noticed that there has been a recovery in Canada. Most people in my constituency are not aware that there is a recovery under way. They read about it in the newspapers and they hear it from the Minister of Finance. They hear various corporate leaders talking about recovery signs, that things are looking good, that the recovery is under way, perhaps not as much as anticipated by the Government, but very clearly that there is a recovery in place. The average man and woman in this country has not had a recovery in terms of their own lives. 1 think it is fair to ask, a recovery for whom? Has it been a fair recovery for all Canadians? It has not.
Who were the winners in this Budget? One of the best ways to determine that is to listen a few hours later, after people have had a chance to analyze the Budget, after the smoke has been blown away from all of the hoopla surrounding the Budget. You notice who is cheering today. You notice who the people are who perhaps celebrated last night with champagne because they really appreciated what this Government has done for them.
Unquestionably those in the boardrooms today are happy because more loopholes have been opened by that wonderful tax loophole man, the Minister of Finance. Again the corporate sector has a number of tax grants and concessions coming its way. There is another group of Canadians, the wealthy elite of Canada, who have had a number of loopholes opened for them as well. Whereas a few days ago we had 200 identifiable tax loopholes, we now have a few more added to make the tax system more unfair and, consequently, the recovery more unfair.
Do we hear any cheers this morning from the 1.5 million Canadians out of work? You notice absolute silence in the country coming from the unemployed because in this Budget there is not a single item that will assist those 1.5 million Canadians who are unemployed today to find meaningful work in the months ahead. Do we hear cheers and accolades coming from the poor of Canada? Do we hear cheers coming from the women of Canada? Do we hear cheers coming from the single women of this country, those involved in the fishery or the forest workers of Canada?
If you listen carefully, do you hear cheers coming from the small business sector? For a handful, yes, but the majority of small businesses in this country are not cheering this morning. After hearing the rhetoric of the Minister of Finance and having done their analysis of what is in the Budget for them, they Find there is nothing to cheer about.
Aside from the corporate boardrooms today and aside from the cheering upper income earners, the lawyers, doctors, den-
February 16, 1984

tists, veterinarians and chiropractors, who are now able to pay income tax at a lower level than they did the night before, who is cheering? As if there were not already enough loopholes in the tax system to cater to the privileged few in society, the Minister of Finance has opened up a new set of loopholes. Where they paid 33W per cent income tax, they now pay 25 per cent. In other words, the Minister of Finance has put thousands and thousands of dollars into the hands of the upper income people, the doctors and lawyers who are involved in incorporating their businesses and are involved in business ventures.
The question must be asked: Who is going to pay for all of these loopholes that have been provided? Who is going to make up the difference? Somebody has to pay the taxes in this country. Somebody has to pay for all the loopholes for the corporations that have been added and for the additional loopholes for the upper income earners of Canada. Did the Minister of Finance do what people across this country have asked him to do, namely rescind the tax increases that he brought in last April that touched every Canadian family? He did not. Therefore, $200 or $300 will be taken from the pockets of every Canadian family to pay for the additional loopholes provided in the Budget last night.
The Minister of Finance says that we helped young people in this country. The young people should be cheering, but do you hear the young people of this country, particularly those who are out of work, cheering today? When you look carefully at this $150 million that the Minister of Finance has provided for youth unemployment, you see it is the same amount as the little Liberal slush fund that we have been talking about for the last few days. When you analyse that and break it down, how much of the unemployed youth are going to be assisted?
Visualize the unemployed youth of Canada, Mr. Speaker, and apply this particular amount of money. It will provide a 12-month job for only 1.5 per cent of all those unemployed today. It is 1.5 per cent for a single year. What about the hundreds and thousands of young people in the next few weeks and months who will be coming on to the job market seeking employment, those coming out of our universities, colleges, technical, trade and secondary schools? That is the assistance this Government has provided for our unemployed youth. It is a pittance. I do not understand how the Minister of Finance has the courage to stand in his place and say as part of his Budget Speech that he and his Government are going to help the young people with this miserly, this miserable, this minute amount of money.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is $1.3 billion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then the Minister of Finance said: "We are going to help the senior citizens of Canada; we are going to increase the contribution to the guaranteed income supplement". A few months ago the Minister of Finance assembled a task force to talk to people across the country to try to understand the needs of senior citizens and to make recommendations to the Gov-
The Budget-Mr. Riis
ernment. The task force did that. It said the beginning step this Government should take was to increase the GIS immediately by $100 a month. Did the Minister do that? No, he did not do that. He provided half of that.
Let us break it down. The senior citizens of Canada on GIS will receive an increase on July 1 this year of 75 cents a day. My parents are senior citizens. I phoned them and said: "Great news, Mom and Dad; you are going to get 75 cents a day starting July 1 from the Minister of Finance". They were not particularly pleased. This means that still today as a result of this so-called improvement for the senior citizens of Canada, hundreds and thousands of them will still be living below the poverty line, the poverty line as described by the Government of Canada. Hundreds and thousands of our senior citizens will be in this situation. Is there anything in this Budget for the war vets, those who fought in Dieppe? No. there is not a thing. Is there any increase for our war vets, people we know who are struggling to survive? No, there is nothing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They get the GIS.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are hundreds and thousands of senior citizens living below the poverty line and the Minister of Finance and the Government says it is going to make a significant contribution to pensions. Then, of course, comes the RRSPs. This will be the real saviour for people's pension systems. When you look closely, Mr. Speaker, many Canadians can take advantage of the RRSPs. They can put in $1,000 or $2,000, and many people do. But the Minister of Finance did not assist so much the average Canadian taxpayer. He said: "We are going to lift the ceiling to $15,500 a year". If you have an extra $10,000 or $15,000 in loose cash at the end of the year, you can invest that in a pension plan. Those who will benefit to the maximum from this allowance are those people whose incomes are nearly $90,000 a year. Those are the ones who will be able to take advantage of the maximum benefit, those with nearly $90,000 a year.
I do not think there is any question of the hypocrisy of this Government. It brings in this Budget and, as my Hon. Leader suggests, it gives those people an $8,000 tax benefit. But the Government said it has changed its mind now and it is going to send out a signal to labour across the country. The Government is now going to ask labour to join in a co-operative venture in terms of getting the economy back on track. The Government said it has just given tax breaks to its friends in the corporate sector and tax breaks to upper income Canadians; but it is now going to ask labour to join in the recovery program. As a first gesture, the Government said it is going to restore free collective bargaining to the public sector. That is like putting a gun to somebody's head and saying: "Now we are going to start free collective bargaining". It is a Russian roulette approach to this whole business.
The Government said it is going to bargain collectively with labour, but it also said: "If you do not agree with us, if you do not do exactly what we say, we are going to legislate a settlement". Is that free collective bargaining? Is that the kind

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Riis
of gesture that will encourage labour across Canada to be willing to co-operate fully? Is that the kind of signal that the Government wants to send out to labour, putting a gun to their head in so-called free collective bargaining? This budget fails to provide any real hope for middle and low-income Canadians in the months ahead, those Canadians who have not been part of the so-called recovery program to date.
I have to refer for a moment or two to my Progressive Conservative friends. They have gone on at some length about the deficit. They argue whether the deficit should be $27 billion, $29 billion, $31.5 billion and so on. That is their concern. They say they are very concerned about that. But the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) stood in his place the other day and said: "We need to increase defence spending by $300 million". Then the fishery critic said in Vancouver: "We have to help the fishing sector and add another $300 million." In agriculture the Tories say the same thing. The Hon. Member who is the critic for employment suggests that we spend more on job creation. The small business critic says we have to spend more on tax concessions to small business. The industry critic stands up daily in this House and says: "We have to provide more and more tax concessions to the corporate sector to encourage it to invest".
You cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. You cannot have individual Members standing up day after day saying spend millions of more dollars here, hundreds of millions of dollars there and billions more in tax concessions, and then say that we have to reduce the deficit. If they were being honest and truthful to the people and were going to assist those sectors as they say they will, and if they are going to reduce the deficit, do you know, Mr. Speaker, who will suffer as a result of that? Do you know who will have their pensions cut? Do you know who will reduce unemployment insurance and reduce assistance to single parents? The Progressive Conservatives.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Baloney!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You cannot have it both ways. You cannot have a reduced deficit and increased spending in virtually every sector. They have to come clean. That is why the Government is being told these days by Progressive Conservatives that they are not going to tell them what they are going to do.
I have to give credit to the Hon. Member who was the previous Minister of Finance in the Conservative Government, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). I have to give him credit for being honest with the people of Canada. He stood up and said: "We cannot tell you what we are going to do. We are unable to tell you what our policies are, because if we did, the people of Canada would never vote for us". He is an honest man; he is an honest John.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am pleased to share a spot on this side of the aisle with such an honest, straightforward Conservative.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were there in 1979. Why did you vote against us?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to pause here in my comments to supplement the amendment provided by the Hon. Member for St. John's West. I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end of the last sentence to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words: "and this House condemns the government for continuing the Liberal-Conservative policies that have produced record mumbers of unemployed, widespread poverty among our elderly, and burdensome taxation for middle and low income Canadians; and this House further condemns the government for failing to introduce in this budget a fair recovery programme that would end unproductive tax concessions to corporations, rescind the $1.4 billion in consumer tax increases announced in the last budget, provide for mechanisms to deal fairly with job displacement resulting from technological change, and increase productive investments in those sectors of the economy which will be the backbone of any future economic prosperity".
Having made the comments I did about my friends in the Conservative Party that they are not prepared to be honest with the people of Canada in terms of their policies, and while we in the New Democratic Party have criticized the Government and the Minister of Finance for not taking the action we felt was required at this time to ensure a fair recovery and have criticized the Conservatives for being vague, I feel obligated to put on the record some of the recommendations we would have put in this Budget. We hope that the Government will consider them in its next budget which it will bring in before another election.
The first thing we would do would be to rescind the increased taxes to consumers. On many occasions we have heard that we need to have a consumer-led recovery; that it is important for Canadians to be able to purchase the homes they need, the appliances they need and the vehicles they require in order to provide stimulus to the manufacturing sector that will enable plants to operate at more than the present 60 per cent or 70 per cent capacity. To that end people must have disposable income to afford these kinds of necessities.
The thing that must not be done, as was done by the Conservative Government during the depression, is to increase taxes. Yet the Minister of Finance is quite prepared to say that taxes on every Canadian household will be increased between $200 and $300 this year, as if that will assist in the recovery program. The first thing this Party would do would be to rescind this tax increase.
In an effort to deal with the deficit, we would then reform the personal income tax system so that everyone would pay their fair share. On many occasions we have pointed out that thousands and thousands of Canadians with incomes of $50,000 per year or $100,000 per year or $500,000 per year do not pay any income tax at all. Then who pays? The 16 million average Canadians who file tax returns each year whose tax is deducted at source pay. They pick up the shortfall and pay more than their fair share. The personal income tax system should be changed so that everyone pays a fair share of the tax burden.
February 16, 1984

The corporate tax system must also be revamped. In the past year many corporations have made hundreds of millions of dollars in profits. We have nothing against that; we like to see a healthy economy. But if a company is going to make hundreds of millions of dollars in profit, as the Bank of Montreal did last year, then we expect it to pay its fair share of income tax and not, as some firms have been able to do through tax loopholes, avoid paying a single red cent in income tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I have to interrupt the Hon. Member because his time has expired. Of course, he could continue his remarks with the unanimous consent of the House. It is agreed?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we would be delighted to agree. I know the Hon. Member is getting into the positive part of his speech and we would like to hear that. I would simply remind him that we have a speaker on this side who would like to talk before lunchtime.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I want to thank my colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party and the Liberal Party for their positive gesture. I will keep my remarks brief and finish my speech in the next few minutes.
As my Leader has suggested on many occasions, Mr. Speaker, one of the ways to deal with the deficit would be to reconsider some of the $10 billion presently handed out in tax concessions and grants to the corporate sector. I do not think it is unfair to say to the corporate sector that if it expects the taxpayers of Canada to assist it in certain ways through tax concessions or grants, some accountability is required. We are entitled to expect some kind of performance either through research and development initiatives, job creation, job training, or the purchase of new plant and equipment from Canadian suppliers. In other words, tax concessions should be tied to a meaningful contribution to the economy. I cannot imagine that anyone would seriously argue against that. I believe the corporate sector would welcome that initiative.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Instead of a free lunch.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We could do away with the free lunches. We are against the concept of simply giving out grants and expecting nothing in return.
Something that has been overlooked in the Budget and has not been commented upon as yet by the Official Opposition is interest rates. In this Party we feel that we cannot have real, sustained economic recovery with interest rates at their present level and with the potential for volatility that we have seen in the last months and years. It is now appropriate for the Minister of Finance, through the Bank of Canada, to take active, positive steps to reduce the interest rates and maintain them at lower levels. The spread between the inflation rate and the interest rate in this country is greater today than ever before in our history. It is time the difference was reduced and interest rates brought down so that people can afford mort-
The Budget-Mr. Deniger
gages and expand their small businesses, their farms, ranches and various economic endeavours. This is the kind of major and bold step that members of the New Democratic Party feel is absolutely necessary for a sustained recovery.
We would also like to expand the job development potential in key sectors of the economy by investing in the infrastructure of those sectors. In simpler terms, the forest industry, for example, is important all across the country. In five out of ten provinces it is a major industry and it is a significant industry in every province, yet it is in dire straits. It is suffering from lack of private and public investment. Is there a better time to invest public sector money in the development of reforestation or the development of salmonid enhancement programs of salmon habitat protection? We do not call this government spending but, rather, serious investment in the economy of Canada.
That is what is required and it must be done next year or within two or three years. We say now is the time to do it because such investment would put hundreds of thousands of Canadians to work immediately in jobs that would bring about a sustained recovery and economic development. In turn, this would generate an increase in tax revenues through corporate and personal income tax for federal coffers. That is the kind of investment we would like to see.
We would like the Government to do some planning. It should sit down with the private sector, with labour and with regional governments to plan what we want to accomplish in the next ten years. It should set out a strategy for the economy and regional strategies that everyone can support and identify with. In that way we could get on with developing the economy. This reeling and wheeling from crisis to crisis, this stumbling about, this ad hockery in terms of economic development, is not good enough. The Budget that was introduced a few hours ago is just one more step in the same direction. There is a lack of vision, a lack of concept or vision about what the country could and should be doing.
This Party feels that the Budget demonstrates that most Canadians have not been heard, Mr. Speaker. Their concerns must be taken into account in these difficult times, their plight must be unveiled and their interest must be represented in the House of Commons.
Today and in subsequent days during this debate the New Democratic Party will represent those voices. The people of Canada have been left out of this document.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!
