subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, budget speeches and Throne Speeches are opportunities for government to reset the course and the direction in which we are

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
travelling. Many of us have felt for some time that we are on the wrong course, travelling in the wrong direction, down a slippery road, and that there is no return.
We have seen the results of philosophical and academic tinkering with our economy. Our national debt has climbed to unacceptable levels. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), pointed out, the interest burden that the average Canadian will pay will be with us for many years. In fact, the Government will have to go to the same money market that the private sector has to tap and that will make things more difficult for private sector financing.
We have seen inflation and recession, and we have seen crippling interest rates ruin hundreds of thousands of business enterprises and shatter the hopes and dreams of millions of Canadians.
1 always approach the period leading up to budget day with anticipation. It is a chance for change, a chance to redress, a chance to restructure. So it was with this Budget. I saw opportunities for the Government to make some changes that could attempt to solve the difficulties facing the 1.5 million unemployed in the country. All those hopes and anticipations were tempered somewhat with information we received from Statistics Canada on January 31 which showed that the recovery appeared to lose some of its vitality in the fourth quarter and that this slowdown would continue early in 1984. The Conference Board of Canada forecast that there were worrisome signs that the recovery may not be as robust as might be expected. The gross domestic product fell by .2 per cent in November and the final demand actually fell by .2 per cent in the third quarter.
From comments reported in newspapers and speeches made by business leaders and others, we see that consumer confidence seems to have fallen in the last quarter. In fact, the survey of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, released in December, shows a further reduction in the levels of capital investment by larger firms for 1984.
I read with great interest of the wide consultation the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) had with the business community in the past several months. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, the Canadian Organization of Small Business Inc. and numerous other business and commercial associations presented briefs and had conversations with the Minister of Finance and his officials.
I know it is easy to look at the headlines in the financial papers and see that this corporation and that corporation posted record profits. But that is not common throughout industry in general, Mr. Speaker. The business community faces many difficulties. While interest rates have modified to some extent, bank rates are still 6.5 percentage points above the level of inflation. When you compare that to where they were prior to the recession, you find that at that time the prime rate was 3.4 per cent above the level of inflation. While inflation has subsided, the spread between inflation and the prime rate has increased. In fact, when we look at real interest rates we see they are double what they really should be. Many
of our financial institutions are very liquid. They have lots of money to lend, but that money is not going to commercial operations. In fact, commercial loans are down substantially.
The real competition for that money is in the residential mortgage field. I think we are all thankful for that. Residential mortgage rates dropped dramatically in the past year. There is no evidence of any increase in commercial loans as far as we can see at this time. There is a reason for this condition, Mr. Speaker. Most of our small and medium-sized businesses are debt financed today, rather than equity financed. They are reluctant to take on any additional long-term debt because of the disastrous interest rate experience they had during the recession. Many companies barely survived.
I know that those who are familiar with the balance sheets and financial statements of business will appreciate that when you look at the balance sheets of these companies you find that they are in a very precarious state. Most companies stripped their earned surplus accounts in order to stay alive during the recession. Many have eaten into their capital accounts and are operating today with very reduced working capital. I believe that is an accurate assessment of the large number of small and medium-sized businesses in the country. That is why commercial loans are down, Mr. Speaker. They are in a delicate condition. They are afraid that if there is a slight bump up in the interest rates, a lot of those companies which survived the recession will not survive a second round. They are hanging on by their fingernails hoping that interest rates will continue to subside. That is one of the things they were looking for and I was looking for in the Budget.
If small and medium-sized businesses are to survive and invigorate themselves and put most of the 1.5 million unemployed to work-the Minister of Finance has said again and again that he is looking to the private sector to help reduce unemployment-that cannot be done if companies have weak balance sheets. It cannot be done if they do not have a working capital with which to go forward, and it cannot be done if there is the slightest chance that interest rates will rise and that the very precarious recovery they have survived is any way in doubt. With the depleted capital account and reduced working capital and debt financing, firms just cannot pick up the slack and hire the unemployed people that the Minister expects.
While the initiatives taken for small business in the Budget will be welcome when they are in place, the structural problem will remain and will discourage the expansion we need to take up the unemployment challenge.
I am most discouraged that the Minister did not move in the matter of capital cost allowance. I think that was a major mistake. I know that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association lobbied very hard for this, and I know from comments 1 have had from business people across the country that they were all looking for some redress in this matter. The fact that it was not done is of great concern to many people. Those who do not understand how a capital cost allowance works will not understand how badly it has hurt the cash flow of most of the businesses that utilize it. The decision not to redress the capital
February 16, 1984

cost allowance has damaged the cash flow of thousands of businesses. It is the main deterrent to capital investment and is hobbling the expansion of industry.
In the Budget the Minister recognized the importance of productivity and noted the high cost of new productive machinery. Our industries must modernize and they require new productive machinery in order to be competitive in world markets. It is frustrating that although the problem was recognized, nothing really was done. Indeed, the forecast for unemployment shows that it will stay in the double digits for the foreseeable future.
An examination of the Budget documents reveals that the Government's forecast of productivity is that it will decline in the next few years. Everyone knows that we are almost at the bottom of the list on the productivity scale of the OECD.
The other thing that we noticed in the Budget was that there was no plan to reduce the deficit beyond the pious words of the Minister. Those of us who have been here a few years have all heard the Minister stand in his place and say that the deficit is going to go down and that, indeed, the Estimates will be tabled in another couple of weeks. Those Estimates may in fact show that government spending is off, but those are the Main Estimates. As we go down the road, we receive Supplementary Estimates (A), (B), (C) and (D), and by the end of this fiscal year, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that our spending will probably be as high or higher than it is right now. Therefore, I get the feeling from the performance of the Minister that he sort of casts himself in the role of a Minister of Finance holding back the hordes of irresponsible spenders who would spend untold billions in order to buy favour from the electorate.
We have seen in the House recently some rather sleazy tactics used by an arrogant Government which is trying to raise its profile with the voting public. And I made reference to those special projects which were apparently privy to Liberal Members of Parliament but not to all Hon. Members of Parliament.
1 must say, Sir, that I was dismayed and angered by the officials in the Department of Finance who attended the lock-up preceding the Budget address to answer questions which arose as a result of our examination of the Budget document. I will not name the individuals. I would not do that. We agreed not to do that. However, I found, Sir, when they were asked tough, precise questions, they sidestepped them by saying, "Well, that is a policy matter and you will have to discuss that with the Minister". When asked for an explanation of some of the numbers we had just seen in the documents, they waffled on those answers as well. In fact, I asked them how much it would cost to repair and put the capital cost allowance provision back to what it was before it was cut in the previous Finance Minister's Budget. The official just put his hand up in the air and pulled down a figure of $1.2 billion. For months I had asked the former Minister of Finance to supply me with that figure. I did not even receive an acknowl-
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
edgement of my letters. It was always going to come when I spoke to him, but it never did. When I pursued, with the official of the Department of Finance, the question of where he got that $1.2 billion, what was the back-up data for that, could he verify it in some way, he finally admitted it was just a guess on his part and he had no real date to back it up at all.
I find that quite a disgusting performance under the circumstances. I had the feeling that those officials were there just to slough us off and not really to answer questions at all but just to give us whatever answer they thought we would accept. They knew that we had to leave at a specified time, so it was just an exercise of the clock as far as they were concerned.
The Budget announced a variety of new studies, consultations, and promises of action down the road, and we quite agree with some of them, we think the intitiatives as far as pensions are concerned are good. I wish they could come forward faster than has been promised. However, I believe they are quite good. I was not too impressed with the $50 a month extra which is going to come to senior citizens in two stages, although I know those senior citizens will be glad of it. One can look at that amount in different ways. I heard someone say it was the equivalent of $1 a week. Someone said it was the equivalent of two doughnuts and a coffee. It is not very generous, but I believe, when it is added to the other moneys which those senior citizens receive, it will help some people who really need some assistance.
The Budget announced that we were going to have some assistance for home owners. I would like to spend the last moments of my time in this debate to talk on that particular subject because I did press the matter very hard in the House with the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) and others. 1 must say that I welcome what is being done, but I do not feel that the real problem has really been addressed. The Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) and other Hon. Members in the House have pursued that problem very vigorously. We are thankful for what has been done. I am sure that many home owners will be thankful as well. However, there are approximately 750,000 Canadians who are trapped with high interest rate mortgages. That problem has not been addressed in this Budget. Some of those individuals-I know because I have had correspondence with them-have had the ability to renegotiate those mortgages. Some of the mortgage companies have bent the rules and helped them. However, 1 hope that the Minister, in his negotiations with the mortgage companies, will insist that they address the matter of the individuals who are trapped in those high interest rate mortgages. He should insist, before he gives any concessions whatsoever to them, that this matter be addressed. I believe what was done to many Canadians was disgusting and degrading. I was angered when I saw some of the mortgage documents which were put forth by these companies where, in the mortgage renewal, they wiped aside the actions of the Parliament of Canada and the actions of a provincial legislature, by causing people to waive their rights under the Interest Act of Canada, under the Mortgage Act of Ontario, and under the Mortgage Act of Manitoba. I thought

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
that was a disgusting display of corporate and monetary power.
I hope that when the Minister deals with the mortgage companies, he will say, "Never again are you guys going to act like this and hold people to ransom." Never again should corporate power be used to set aside the decisions of the elected Members of this Parliament or the elected members of a legislature. That was a disgusting display of power and they got away with it. I hope the Minister will take these words to heart and will deal with these companies, and deal with them severely, because there is no way we should give them anything until they agree that they will never take that course of action again.
I say this in particular because in discussing the matter with the officials at the briefing yesterday, I asked them in particular what they meant in their comments about amendments to the Interest Act. One of them told me that the proposal is that the Government is going to amend the Interest Act to remove Section 10 which allows an individual who has had a mortgage for five years to renegotiate that mortgage on the payment of three months' interest. The officials claim that this is the reason why we have short-term mortgages, this is the reason why we do not have 10-year mortgages. I do not know what world they are living in. All they have to do is to travel across the border and see what happened in the United States which has had the same provision for years. There are still 25-year and 30-year mortgages there, and that country still has that provision.
I disagree that we should remove this right from the mortgagors. However, if we are going to remove it, then there has to be a quid pro quo as far as the mortgage companies are concerned. I hope, Sir, that never again will we see in this country the raw corporate power displayed by some of the mortgage and trust companies whereby they ravaged and gutted mortgagors in this country and caused them to lose their homes.
I commend the Government for the action it is taking. However, I believe it should be stronger. But this is a first step and perhaps when the legislation is introduced, we will have an opportunity to speak to it and perhaps we can improve it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a very short comment. The Hon. Member, as usual, has made some strong and careful representations on behalf of people like mortgage holders, and 1 congratulate him for that. I do not want to take away from that. I would just like to add a single point in correction of something the Hon. Member said. He referred to the Opposition and critics' lock-up yesterday afternoon. I would remind the Hon. Member of two things. First, when he went in there and the public officials arrived, they talked to him under the assumption of confidence. They did not talk to him under the assumption that they would be quoted here in the House of Commons. Just the little trick of not mentioning the individual's name does not quite overcome that. Second, he has drawn the inference that the same officials were political creatures. I would like to correct him. We were dealing with impartial public servants, not people from the Liberal Party or from the
Government but impartial public servants who do have to draw a line in their responsibilities between the things they do as public servants and the things he would like to know as an Opposition critic. They have to draw that line and leave it up to the Minister to decide whether to reveal certain information. That is their duty. They have no choice in the matter. The Hon. Member has risen today and left the impression, first, that he was being manipulated for political reasons and, second, that these people are not impartial. I would like to make it clear that both of those points are not correct. Not only that, but I think he damages the general spirit of co-operation by revealing these sorts of things, true or false, from the lock-up, when it is supposed to be confidential.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member will read the record he will find that he is quite wrong. 1 did not mention the word "political" or "political decisions" or make reference to that in any way, shape or form. I did not mention the officials' names; that was part of the confidence that we agreed to. I did not specifically quote directly things that they had said. I said, Mr. Speaker, I was disappointed in the quality of the information they supplied to us, and that they did not answer questions directly. They pulled figures out of the air and they generally sloughed off hard questions that were put to them. I think that is a fair comment. This is not the first lock-up I have been in, there have been several over the years, and in the past we have had more direct and hard information from the people of the Department of Finance than we had yesterday. I was most disappointed and I was drawing a comparison between previous years and this particular year. I say again that I was disappointed in the quality of information that they passed on to us. They may as well not have been there as far as I was concerned. I do not think anyone who was there really got very much out of it at all.

speakeroldname: Hon. David Smith (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like at the outset to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) for presenting this House yesterday with what I believe to be a very optimistic Budget. I call it an optimistic Budget because, first of all, of its evaluation of the Canadian spirit. I call it an optimistic Budget because of the open consultative process that took place in its development, and because it reaffirms the role of this Government in helping those who need help the most. 1 would also like to thank the Minister of Finance for asking me to be one of the first speakers in this debate. I think he has done that because, quite frankly, my responsibilities as Minister for Small Business are made easier because of this Budget. This Budget, Mr. Speaker, is a good Budget for small business. It recognizes the vital role played by the small business sector in the economic recovery taking place throughout this country.
Small business, Mr. Speaker, is really the lifeblood of the Canadian economy. There are 750,000 small businesses in Canada. They make up 97 per cent of the business firms in this country. They represent 30 per cent of the business sector of the Gross National Product. They represent 42 per cent of the private sector jobs in this country. The people of Canada who own and run small businesses believe in this country. They believe in the economic future of this country because they have invested in it. They believe in the free enterprise system. They believe in initiative, the work ethic, in taking risk, and they believe in enjoying the rewards of hard work. Those are the people who make up the small business sector of this country, and this Government believes in them. Our confidence in that small business sector is well placed because at the moment they are creating about two thirds of the new jobs being created in this country. One of the major objectives of the Minister of Finance's Budget was to create jobs through partnership with the private sector.
I submit that this Budget represents a balanced Budget, balanced in the sense that it represents sound economic planning on the one hand and is socially responsible on the other hand. That is understandable because that is the philosophy of this Government. This is a Government which believes in the free enterprise system and also believes in social justice within it.
Before going into some of the areas which I think benefit the small business sector, I would like to state that, contrary to what some cynics may think, this is not an election Budget, not a Budget based on opinion polls, not an attempt to score
The Budget-Mr. Smith
political points against an Opposition which is bereft of any ideas of its own. It is a balanced Budget, a reflective Budget, a thoughtful Budget and a responsible Budget. It represents sound economics with a social conscience.
How does that philosophy contrast with the philosophy of the Conservative Party? We look at their critic, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). What did he say? He said, "You have to be tough, mean, nasty and do all kinds of unpleasant things. That is why I am not going to outline what these things would be now". Do you believe it? He actually said that. We all know that he believes it, but that he would actually say it is a bit unthinkable. He went on to say that a Conservative Budget at this time would scare Canadians. That is what the official critic for the Conservative Party said. Well, Mr. Speaker, this Government is not out to scare Canadians. It is out to build confidence in the economic recovery we have seen taking place in this country. That is the difference between us and the Official Opposition. Listen to the Hon. Member's words: "You have to be tough, mean and nasty". Well, there is no doubt in my mind that if they were ever in office they would be tough, mean and nasty. They were before, and God help Canadians if they are in there again because that is exactly what they can expect.
Before reviewing some of the provisions of this Budget that I think are of particular benefit to the small business sector, I would like to say a word about the process. The basic theme this Budget process represents is consultation with the private sector, consultation with all elements of the small business sector, business organizations and numerous submissions from private individuals. These submissions have been reviewed, considered by officials and the Minister of Finance, and in some cases they have been accepted. One of the issues on which the Government has received many representations in recent years, and in recent months in particular, has to do with the whole question of the complexity of the tax system. A complex tax system can be time consuming and expensive to deal with. The Minister of Finance responded to that concern. There are specific changes to the tax system which simplify it. I will not go into all the proposals, such as the elimination of the accumulative deduction account, but in addition we have a very thorough paper which has been released called Simplifying Taxes for Small Business which will permit the maximum amount of discussion and consultation with all elements of the Canadian business community. I think it is possible that some fine-tuning may occur and some further changes may take place as a result of that consultative process.
The Canadian Tax Foundation and L'Association Quebe-coise de Planification Fiscale et Successorale played important roles in consultations. They organized a couple of symposiums and conducted an ongoing dialogue with officials of the Minister of Finance. On the whole question of the specific changes with regard to tax simplification, over two-thirds of the amount of legislation relating to the tax rules for small business have been eliminated. That is real progress, Mr. Speaker,

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Smith
which everyone in the House should be pleased with and quite proud of.
The purpose of the further discussions is really twofold. It is, first of all, to solicit non-expert input and to assure a continuity to these changes so that taxpayers themselves can live with them. It is also to allow the Government through this process to discuss these proposals in greater depth before they are implemented. As 1 said, it is possible that some further changes may take place as a result of those consultations.
There are other general Budget changes which dramatically benefit the small business sector. This Budget is great for small business. These changes include the easing of the tax installment payments. There are 50,000 small businesses and family farm corporations in the country which will benefit from that change. There are the auto standby charge, the administrative improvements in the sales tax, the longer appeal period for tax appeals, the provisions which permit the awarding of costs for legal fees in successful tax litigation cases and still more benefits, and the opportunity for many small businesses in the country which want to take advantage of Third World business opportunities to receive assistance from the $1.3 billion aid trade fund. Another aspect of the Budget which benefits the small business sector is the continuation of the fight against inflation, and the 4 per cent price guideline ceiling.
There are other areas of interest in the Budget which relate to my Cabinet duties. I would like to say a word about tourism. This Budget is good for tourism. The Budget reaffirms the Government's commitment to the Special Recovery Capital Projects Program. More than $1 billion is being spent on these projects. A number of them do relate to the tourist industry and improvements to the tourist industry in the country. A large proportion of businesses in the tourist industry are small businesses. What is good for small business is good for tourism. In the recent Throne Speech, the Government clearly recognized this and announced that a tourism strategy was being developed and would be introduced before too long. The Government recently announced some television campaigns, one to encourage Canadians to vacation in this country, and another one, which will be starting in a couple of months, to encourage Americans to visit Canada. The tourism industry will also be enhanced by these various programs. We also have access in the tourism industry to the new Industrial Regional Development Program which is operated by our Department.
An exciting area of the Budget, Mr. Speaker, is the proposal to encourage employees to participate actively in the economic recovery of the country through stock options and profit sharing. The rationale of this proposal is quite sound. First of all, it provides an incentive for greater productivity. In other words, it gives both management and labour an incentive to increase productivity and profits. It will also improve employer and employee relationships and go a long way to encouraging an entrepreneurial attitude among Canadians.
In my opening remarks I mentioned that this Budget represents a balance. It is balanced, on the one hand, by sound
economic planning and, on the other hand, by a commitment to our social responsibilities. The latter is evidenced by the improvements to pensions and the raising of the Guaranteed Income Supplement payments. Both of these policies reaffirm the Government's traditional commitment to living up to our social responsibility.
Another provision which relates to the question of pension security, and is of great interest to the small business sector, has to do with the lifting of the ceilings on the RRSPs. This is very important to many small businessmen who are not part of big pension schemes that are often available to people in large companies or in the public sector. These ceilings have been lifted to $10,000 in 1985 and they will be rising to $15,500 in 1988. This is clearly something from which small business will benefit considerably.
I would like to make a few comments about the improvements to the Government's policies with regard to pensions. Proposed improvements include the splitting of pension benefits upon marriage breakdown, the continuation of survivor benefits on remarriage, and the ensuring of equal pensions for men and women retiring under the same circumstances. I understand that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) will be introducing the appropriate amendments shortly after consultations with the provinces.
Another topic which I welcome is the discussion of a homemaker's pension. It is a priority of the Government that women receive adequate retirement income. These measures will be one way of ensuring that. The proposed changes to improved RRSPs will also greatly increase the flexibility and access to tax assistance for small business persons saving for retirement.
Complementing this focus on women in the home are studies done by the small business secretariat on women's role in the labour force. While the trend of women entering the business world is a relatively recent one, small businesses owned and operated by women are quite large employers, especially of other women. I recently saw statistics which suggested that about 30 per cent of the small businesses in the country are controlled by women, a lot of them in the retail trade. About two-thirds of the women surveyed by the secretariat felt that female business owners do not face problems which are any different from businesses in general. Women wish to be treated as equal members of the business community, and equality of treatment is something which I can assure you is my goal and the goal of the Government.
I am optimistic, Mr. Speaker, that the Finance Minister's emphasis on small business will have the desired spin-off effect and stimulate the overall economy. When you talk of small business, you are talking about all kinds of different enterprise. You are talking about small manufacturers and processors and the construction sub-trades. Of course, the whole home construction industry will greatly benefit from the Mortgage Rate Protection Program which was introduced. We are also talking about tourism operators. There are lots of small hotel operators and restaurateurs who certainly will find many of these provisions relating to small business of great benefit to them. I
February 16, 1984

am optimistic that the great Canadian resource, which we call small business, is receiving the encouragement appropriate to its role in the economy.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate what I perceive to be the three major themes of the new Budget of the Minister of Finance. They are, first of all, a Budget process which is based on a consultative process with all the sectors of the community, and in particular the private sector, big business, small business and everyone in the business community. Second, there is a thrust to increase productivity and our ability to compete. Third, there is the recognition of the small business sector as the main source of entrepreneurship, risktaking and job creation. I might also add, Mr. Speaker, that I, other Ministers, and particularly the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren), will be continuing an ongoing process of consultation with the business sector, including the small business sector, to further the goals of this Budget.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Minister of Finance for presenting what I consider to be a sound, responsible, upbeat Budget. It is an optimistic Budget which represents sound economic planning on the one hand with a social conscience on the other hand. It includes programs and initiatives that display in the finest way the role that the Government can play in supporting the economic recovery that we see under way throughout Canada at this time. I might say that I would also like to thank the Minister of Finance for the opportunity to participate in this debate at its outset.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the speech of the Minister of State for Small Business Mr. Smith in which he pointed out the virtues of small business. I think he indicated accurately that a great deal of the job creation that we hope will occur in this country in the next few years will in fact come from that small business sector. Perhaps it would be even more accurate to say that all of the new jobs created in Canada in the next decade will come through the medium and small business sector.
Mr. John Bullock is President of perhaps the largest small business organization in Canada and the most effective lobbyist on the important issues of the small business community. He is someone who has gained respect from the Minister and the respect of the small business community in general because of his grasp of the reality of that particular sector. How does the Minister interpret a comment Mr. Bullock made last night in his response to the Budget when he indicated that this Budget will not result in any new job creation in the small business sector? He indicated that he was pleased with a number of housekeeping changes that had been made for which the small business community had been lobbying for a number of years. The Minister went to some length to explain what some of these improvements were.
In terms of job creation, the most powerful small business lobby in Canada has stated that the Budget will result in no
The Budget-Mr. Smith
new jobs being created in the small business sector. How does the Minister respond to that comment?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sometimes I agree with Mr. Bullock and sometimes I do not. Mr. Bullock made a number of comments last night, not all of which were recorded. Some of them were supportive of the measures in the Budget and some were not.
I happen to have a different opinion. I believe the Budget is responsible. By making it easier for the small business community to operate in a number of ways, it will inevitably result in jobs being created.
If one looks at the reaction to the Budget by business leaders as a whole, it is quite positive. As a matter of fact, there are a number of officials in Mr. Bullock's organization, the Federation of Independent Business, who commented on the Budget. If I might use a word that is sometimes used by the other side of the House, if one looks at the totality of their comments, on balance they are quite positive and supportive.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the Minister comment on the $1,000 that the Government will now refund to a small business that successfully appeals a tax decision as a way of compensating the cost? He knows that the average cost incurred by a small business in this country when it appeals a tax decision averages between $2,000 and $4,000. Why would the Government not refund the legitimate costs of small businesses when the small businesses in these cases have been proven to be honest and straightforward but it was the Government that had erred? Rather than the $1,000, why not reimburse what we know is a more realistic cost?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are many things we would like to do that I suppose would be popular, but we must look at all these matters from the perspective of the Government's ability to afford them. I suggest that changing the rules to permit the courts to award costs of up to $1,000 is a good start. I think it is one that should be applauded and welcomed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister with respect to small business. In the area that I represent, the Federal Business Development Bank has taken on the name among all the small businesses in that community of the "Federal Business Destruction Bank".
There are some extremely serious problems with respect to small business getting involved in recovery. The bank has refused to refinance loans which would bring them down from interest rates that are as high as 21 per cent. It is only talking about bringing refinancing down to 14 per cent or 16 per cent, and it is only willing to do so by imposing a substantial penalty, even though it is prepared to add it on to the interest rate. TThis is causing some extremely serious problems for small businesses in the area that I represent, and I assume right across the country.
There is a group of small businessmen in that community who are forming a committee to become involved in a fight against the Federal Business Development Bank. Can the

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Smith
Minister tell me and others what action he will take to make that Federal Business Development Bank more responsive to the needs of small businesses over a period of time in order to help them back on the road to recovery? Is he prepared to fight for the same results that the Minister of Finance talked about in aiding home owners to refinance? What will he do about the Government's bank that is harming business so badly?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the bank is doing exactly that. There are 85 branches of the bank throughout Canada. To a large extent they represent a lender of last resort.
However, the bank is still dealing with public funds and must do so in a responsible manner. It cannot give out loans on the basis of political considerations. It has to give them on the basis of banking considerations.
No one is forced to take a loan from the Federal Business Development Bank. When someone takes a loan from any bank, it is a contract. At the time the bank issues those funds, it must secure those funds and it does so at a certain interest rate. It seems to me to be an unreasonable request to the bank to say that it would then have to suffer the loss for refinancing.
I might say that the FBDB had losses in the last fiscal year of approximately $80 million. I do not think anyone could suggest for one second that the FBDB has not been taking its part of the responsibility in providing financing to a number of firms that are unable to go anywhere else in the country. That does not mean that we just abandon all banking principles and give money away.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member on his elevation to the Cabinet. I have felt for some time that the federal Department of Tourism has not had a sufficiently high profile. Tourism is a tremendous industry in this country and many people do not realize its importance.
Does the Hon. Minister have any funds with which he can help build unique attractions that will bring people to the country? These funds could be given either on a loan or a grant basis. 1 am not talking about ordinary projects but about something that is unique in the country. Is there such a federal fund for that and, if not, what is the primary function of the federal Department of Tourism?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the primary function of Tourism Canada is to encourage tourism in this country. Of course, we do not try to favour one area of the country over another. We encourage Canadians to vacation in Canada and try to give equal coverage to all areas of the country that represent tourist destinations.
We also do a lot of advertising outside of Canada. In April we will launch a major television campaign in the northern tier of the United States, aimed at encouraging tourists to this country.
I welcome the Hon. Member's interest in tourism. 1 might say that the Industrial Regional Development Program, which is administered by the Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Lumley), does provide some assistance to the establishment of what may be tourist related proposals. If the Hon. Member wants me to provide him with more information or to set up a meeting with interested parties who have some ideas, I would be happy to do that with the appropriate officials.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the new young Cabinet Minister. It concerns small business. It is a question about a group of people whom I consider to be some of the most important small business people we have, those in the business of food production. 1 am aware that the Government has made some provision in the area of capital gains, but I consider its efforts to be rather insignificant.
Bearing in mind that valuation day was established in 1971, how can this Government or any government continue to take the view that in fact it has the legitimate right to calculate gain as gain when in fact it takes inflation from 1971 to whenever the calculation is made and calls it gain? Any child in grade five knows that the Government is really causing double taxation and therefore putting small business persons, be they farmers or otherwise, into a very difficult and unfair situation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly had no objection to allowing ten minutes more. I realize that a number of Members would have liked to put some pertinent questions to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism). Well, Standing Orders are Standing Orders!
Mr. Speaker, I have some comments on the Budget. In fact, this morning, in the newspapers, the Budget was hardly as popular as the news that Gaetan Boucher won this major international event. You will understand that Canadians were very interested in this major win and were more excited about a Canadian winning than about the Budget, considering the bill we got yesterday from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Mr. Speaker, I was listening earlier to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and I do not doubt his good faith and his plans to increase co-operation with the private sector. He was expressing his Government's faith in the private sector in this respect. Even the provinces, perhaps! However, Mr. Speaker, I am astounded that the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) should fail to realize that the Minister of Finance, who produced this pile of infor-
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
mation, measures and proposals in the House yesterday, has been behaving for at least ten years with incredible arrogance. Considering his forecasts for the energy and financial sectors, I would say not only arrogance but also unprecedented incompetence. And now they are talking about restoring a climate of confidence! I wonder they even dare to talk about restoring a climate of confidence, when over the last eighteen months, and I am positive about this and I have the polls to prove it, Mr. Speaker, this Government has lost the confidence of the general public. Just over 30 per cent, on average, over the last 18 months! This proves Canadians no longer have confidence in this Government. Of course this Government will always say it won a majority in 1980, but during the last eighteen months, the Government knows it lost the confidence of the general public, and it is trying to act as though it had the public's support, and the Minister of Finance is talking with a kind of optimism that reeks of hypocrisy, since he knows perfectly well he no longer has the confidence of the general public and will be unable to restore that confidence with the Budget he brought down yesterday afternoon. Mr. Speaker, for your information, just to prove to what extent the Minister of Finance has lost the confidence of the general public, there are certain people in the business world who told me as a joke: Listen here, La Salle, when you form the Government in a few months, remember to give the Minister of Finance the post he would like to have, which is President of the Canada Post Corporation. Then he could read the mail of all Canadians without any problems. Mr. Speaker, you see the kind of joke the credibility of the Minister of Finance has become, a credibility that has hit its lowest level. Mr. Speaker, it is clear that in this Budget, some measures are more significant than others. There is some good news, since the Government finally decided to increase benefits for the elderly and single persons, so they can meet their financial obligations. Well, Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House we have realized for a long time that this need existed. The Government seems to be willing to do something about it. Considering the measures the Government proposed yesterday, and unless I am mistaken there are only one or two that could be put into effect before January 1, 1985. Mr. Speaker, as you and I are aware, the likelihood that there will be a general election before January 1, 1985 is considerable. So, in his hypocrisy, the Prime Minister goes on and gives us a scenario he will probably not be responsible for putting into effect. Mr. Speaker, I suppose there is also reason to rejoice that they finally realized what a problem the Revenue Canada tax forms were for small and medium-sized businesses. It seems the Government has finally decided to change and improve the tax forms for small and medium-sized businesses, but I hope nobody will assume, Mr. Speaker, that this is going to create thousands of jobs. It will help small and medium-sized businesses in that the forms will be easier to understand and much easier to complete. So, of course, we are pleased with this change.

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
There is also a reference to assistance to farmers. It is perfectly obvious, Mr. Speaker, that before even considering legislation that would help farmers give up for and benefit from a pension, they would first have to start making money and have some kind of security. Perhaps they should have considered appropriate measures for stimulating recovery in the agricultural sector. The survival of agriculture is a very important issue, and it is one the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has failed to address. It is therefore clear that the Budget's proposals with respect to farmers are quite inadequate, and it is also clear that the Minister has decided against considering a single aspect of a major problem today, which is financing. Many farmers are still faced with the exorbitant mortgage rates that prevailed a few years ago, and unemployment is also a problem. I see no specific measures in the Budget aimed at helping those farmers-and every Member of this House is aware of the situation-at saving them from bankruptcy and giving them the security they need to improve their circumstances, and at improving the state of the agricultural sector in this country.
[DOT] (WOO)
Mr. Speaker, the Budget also proposes to provide some kind of insurance for mortgage rates. Details are not available yet, and the Minister indicated that program criteria will be announced within a month. There is indeed a pressing need, Mr. Speaker, for a measure of security and stability, and the Minister of Finance was not saying anything new when he mentioned this in the Budget yesterday. For many years and many months we have been urging the Government to take action in this particular area and to strengthen the construction industry, which is a vital part of our economy.
And then, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance spoke very eloquently about helping unemployed young people. The new Minister of State for Youth did admit recently that young Canadians are driven to despair, that we are in the process of wasting a whole generation, and she said that quite simply as she was assuming her new responsibilities as Minister. Well now, Mr. Speaker, for the past 15 years this Government was supposed to look after youth, it was supposed to create jobs, something which would have given those young people a much brighter outlook on life than the one they have now.
It would seem that the Government has just realized that between 400,000 and 500,000 young Canadians are now seeking employment and going through a desperate crisis, so the Minister, of course, starts throwing millions of dollars at the problem, $150 million more! But, Mr. Speaker, suppose all that money is spent or earmarked for programs such as we had before, programs which at best would mean jobs for 15 to 20 per cent of young people for periods ranging from 20 to 26 weeks. Perhaps the lucky ones will indeed work for 52 weeks. But at the end of the programs those young people will have to draw unemployment insurance benefits, just as they have been doing now for the past four or five years. Fet us be honest, Mr. Speaker, those programs are practically just another name for social welfare. Young people are hired to work on projects which hopefully are worthwhile-but not necessarily so, as you know-and then they go back to unemployment insurance. How can such an attitude on the part of the Government build up the confidence of Canadians? How can the country possibly get back on the road to prosperity with temporary programs offering temporary employment? And the Minister proudly claims that the Canadian Government created 400,000 new jobs last year. Never did he say how many of those jobs were temporary. Thousands of those 400,000 jobs lasted for 20 or 26 weeks, then it was the unemployment line again. A good many people do not even figure in the statistics because they have no jobs and their unemployment benefits are exhausted. The answer to that, of course, is provincial social welfare. How easy it is to fool young people by telling them that we now have a Minister of State for Youth who will look after them. It would seem that there was no need for that over the past 15 years, but now we do have a Department of Youth and we will solve the problem which has been there all along. No way, Mr. Speaker! Young people are not that stupid! They should not be likened to children who have no idea about the responsibilities of Government. This budget fails to meet the aspirations of young Canadians and will do nothing to create jobs.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to underline the fact that the Minister admitted recently that he had been unable to spend the millions of dollars set aside to create jobs in his 1983 budget and that there still remained between $300 million and $400 million to be spent. Naturally, he has to reallocate this money in his new Budget. However, how can he explain the fact that, with respect to the exercise in co-operation or co-ordination with the provinces which he so often mentions, the Government has not yet succeeded in coming to the necessary agreement, not even with my own Province of Quebec? Mr. Speaker, you are aware of the incredible number of jobs lost in Quebec, and I am also aware of the fact that no agreement has been reached yet, and that the necessary efforts have not been made to fulfill the needs of the 1,250 Quebec municipalities which are hoping that an agreement will be signed by the federal and the Quebec Governments. According to my information, and it comes from a good source, this question has now been before the Cabinet for the past few weeks. Yet, the Ministers are themselves from Quebec and there are also well over six dozens of Members of Parliament. All these ministers from Quebec have not seen fit to settle this matter once and for all so that municipal projects which would generate employment may go ahead.
Mr. Speaker, there is one point on which the Minister of Finance is not saying the whole truth, not to say that he is lying to the House. He is not saying the whole truth when he talks about his efforts to create jobs. An agreement could have been signed many months ago; this would have satisfied the municipalities and prevented the Quebec Government from
February 16, 1984

threatening municipalities with penalties because the federal Government wanted to give them grants directly. Co-ordination, co-operation and true respect for federalism imply the respect of provincial jurisdictions. What the Minister of Finance is not saying is that he does not believe in this concept and that the Government does not want to believe in it either, Mr. Speaker! During this Budget debate, I urge the Minister of Finance to realize the importance of signing this agreement on behalf of the 1,250 municipalities which are waiting and hoping that the federal Government will finally set aside its partisan motives and accept to sign an agreement with Quebec, so that these municipalities may receive the federal funds to which they are entitled. The Liberal Members from Quebec, and 1 as a Conservative Member from Quebec, would applaud such an agreement and we would be able to tell the people of Quebec that the taxes that they pay to Ottawa are being redistributed fairly.
On this issue, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the Government has shown a lack of good faith and has not done what was necessary to come to an agreement on a matter as urgent and as important as this one for Quebec. Of course, the Government would rather do what it has been doing these last few months. It would rather use these $250 million allocated to Quebec for something else and launch various projects without providing sufficient information to the Opposition! Mr. Speaker, such a method comes close to corruption. It is unacceptable! The Government would have done better to sign an agreement with Quebec. Of course, the Liberal Members from Quebec were embarrassed when they heard the mayors of certain municipalities and people in Quebec tell them: "Why is it that we cannot benefit from the amounts allocated by the federal Government?" This is why this Government has decided to implement a program which allowed them to allocate certain amounts to Quebec for projects which were most often submitted by party supporters, and at the same time to increase their popularity in Quebec! Indeed, in Quebec like elsewhere in the country, this Government is running short of popular support.
Mr. Speaker, these are some of the comments that we must make in this House.
I pray and urge the Quebec Liberal ministers and caucus members to conclude this agreement without delay; should they refuse next Tuesday-I know they have to deal with this issue at their next Cabinet meeting-there are a number of Quebec Liberal members who are quite unhappy about this absence of agreement, and my information comes from very reliable sources, Mr. Speaker.
Also, the Minister of Finance referred to the coherent stability of his economic policies! How can he expect the business community to take him seriously when he does not seriously raise in his budget the possibility of increasing the amounts allocated to research and development. Mr. Speaker, businessmen and ordinary citizens in Canada are aware that
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
high technology is the key to streamlining our industry, increasing our productivity, reshaping our industry to protect our traditional jobs and create new ones. No increase in the funds allocated to research and development, Mr. Speaker! This is quite revealing! This should be the essential element of any economic policy. How can the Government expect to convince Canadians to devote more money to advanced research, something we need if we want to plan rationally our development on the basis of our needs.
That the Minister of Finance should present this document without First of all using research as the foundation and providing funds for advanced technology is unthinkable. We are well aware that our industries could benefit from export markets if they had the advanced technology they need. In addition, more research could enable union members to understand better the importance of productivity if they want their industry to compete on world markets. Witholding the funds needed for increased research and development is tantamount to ruling out the economic recovery, however urgent it may be.
We talk about better co-operation with the private sector. The Minister of Finance lost all credibility when as Minister of Energy he fought fiercely against the private sector and yet today he is making a desperate appeal to businessmen begging them to take part in that economic recovery. With a rare sense of optimism, he is now referring to economic growth. Mr. Speaker, we are aware of the present conditions. We know that the economic recession was quite painful and I do not agree with the Minister of Finance that we are now on the road to recovery. The Minister cannot obtain the co-operation of the private sector as a result of his recent beahaviour. Mr. Speaker, I heard a while ago and I am now coming to the end of my comments, I heard the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce suggest that a Conservative budget would frighten Canadians. I can tell him right now that thousands of Canadians are asking for a general election to condemn, and rightly so, a government which has so badly failed in all areas.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest the Hon. Member who put the question was absolutely wrong in implying we were not ready to help small and medium businesses. We would give them the same advantages as to all other Canadian businesses. And while small and medium businessmen will appreciate the improved income tax forms, I think this is a good thing but it is not enough. There are tax measures in favour of small and medium businesses we already supported, but what is needed to assist them is finding new markets, conducting better market research abroad, and providing services to increase productivity. For a long time, we have relied on official, theoretical studies done by consultants. I feel the time has come to provide small and medium businesses with in-depth studies to increase their productivity, and competitiveness and lessen their dependence on government grants for survival.
Briefly, we would help the small and medium business sector by showing them how to catch their own fish instead of giving them any.
So much for research. As I said, research subsidies are inadequate. There is no reference to that in the budget, but with additional subsidies, invaluable services could be afforded to the small and medium business sector. We do not want our small and medium businesses run by the State. We want to help them identify markets through the provision of services and even foreign market research. And this is not aimed at multinational corporations only. We are committed to a kind of regional development involving an increasing number of small and medium businesses, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, although the Hon. Member did not deal with the question which involves the protection of small business in the country, I would like to raise another question. On the matter of the multinational friends of the Conservative Party, I would refer the Hon. Member to his Leader's own speeches in which he said that the Conservative Party will facilitate the entry into Canada of foreign companies and foreign investment. Let me use another example to show where his Party is right off track with small business. Into this country have come a number of waste disposal companies, welcomed in with the foreign investment crowd. What they have done is driven the small Canadian companies out of business with their practices.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Name one.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will. There is no competition legislation that is effective in Canada to protect Canadian small businesses from the deep pockets and the predatory practices of those foreign companies. Greater Vancouver is riddled with this problem. People are crying for assistance. The Conservative Party is quite willing to see those small Canadian businesses go down the drain as a result of the unfortunate practices of the foreign-owned corporations in the country. What is that Party prepared to do to control foreign investment so that small Canadian businesses are not driven out?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say in all humility that I have never claimed to be able to answer all questions that are put to me in this House. Contrary, to others, I know my limits, thank God!
However, when the Hon. Member implies that the Progressive Conservative Party is against small and medium size businesses, I regret to tell him, with all due respect, that it is obviously incorrect. We want to protect them. We want to give them every opportunity to survive. Of course, my colleague and myself do not share the same philosophy. I would never want to support businesses which are unprofitable for all practical purposes. However, I want our party and the government, any government, to provide such businesses every possible opportunity to survive and expand, and our party completely agrees with that. That is our position. I would add that if we succeed in providing these opportunities to our small and medium size businesses, to Canadian businesses, we will have greatly reduced the impact of foreign products. Because we must be competitive. And I don't want to hear about locking us up into full-scale protectionism. We must keep some ties with the outside world. On the other hand, I admit and 1 realize that it is important as well to provide a minimum of protection for Canadian trade, but within reasonable limits. The question is to determine what is reasonable and unreasonable.
February 16, 1984

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always find it amusing to hear the socialist from Powell River talk about competition. Nationalism and competition do not go together.
I have a question for the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle). I enjoyed what he said about research and development. It reminded me of an excellent engineer, the Dean of Engineering at the University of Alberta, Dr. Bob Hardy. When I was with the Department of Highways in Alberta, he suggested that if we spent 1 per cent of our budget on research, it would bring back tremendous dividends. We adopted his suggestion and over a ten-year period found that we not only got better value for every dollar but also had better structures and better public works. 1 agree with what the Hon. Member said about research and development.
Are there areas in his particular riding where research and development might bring in more jobs or give better value for every public dollar spent? That is also important.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Indeed, Mr. Speaker, each and every region of Canada would stand to gain a lot more than is the case now if we were getting a better value for our dollars by investing more in research and development. In my riding-and this goes for any riding in Canada-it is obvious that we have to spend more money on research and development, because that will eventually enable us to carry out projects which meet the specific needs of the region.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure for me to join in the debate on the Budget. After a good deal of examination of the documents yesterday when I was privileged to attend the lock-up with Hon. Members from both sides of the House, I became quite enthused about the policies it set out.
We all realize that the federal deficit is very large and is constraining the Government's ability to move. There was no room for the Government to expand expenditures in a major way. Neither was there the option of greatly reducing the deficit at this time because of the fragility of the recovery and the need to move into an expansion phase that would ensure that we do not damage the recovery that is under way and which promises to increase employment and put Canada back on the rails again.
I was very interested to hear the Minister's speech and to hear about these programs. I will deal with them later. I was also interested to know how the Opposition would attack the Budget. It contained measures for small business, for pension reform, a program for mortgage insurance, programs that made sense, tax simplification for small business-all of those made sense and were done with consultation and with the provision for further consultation. It seemed to me that it was going to be difficult for the Opposition to attack these measures.
The Budget-Mr. Evans
When the Opposition finance critic entered the debate last night and again this morning, we did not hear any discussion of the substance of the provisions in the Budget. For 90 minutes the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) talked about one thing-the deficit. He talked about the deficit from every angle that the mind could imagine. It was the subject of a 90-minute discourse by the Hon. Member for St. John's West. There was nothing in his speech about the provisions of the Budget or on the factors which gave rise to the deficit; there was simply a diatribe about all the ills that would befall Canada if the deficit were not dealt with.
There was nothing about what the Conservative Party would do if it were in power or would have done had it been in power during the same period. We should recall-and the Hon. Member for St. John's West raised this in his speech because he knew that we would raise it-that last year when he spoke about the April Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), he was asked what he would do in the circumstances that faced the country then. His response at that time, which he admitted this morning, was that the Minister had taken a responsible position, that it was the right Budget for the time and that basically he would do the same thing. That is what he said last April. What dramatic changes have occurred since then? Last night the Minister of Finance brought forward an extremely responsible Budget, given the conditions that face the country.
In the last year and a half we have been in the midst of a major world recession. This recession hit every industrialized country in the world and hit the less developed countries the hardest. It was the worst world-wide recession since the 1930s. That is the reason for the deficit that we face now. That is the logic of it.
The question then arises, if the deficit is far beyond what a Conservative government would have allowed, how would it have achieved that? I expected to hear the Hon. Member for St. John's West deal with that issue. For example, would the Conservatives have cut unemployment insurance benefits? Would they have cut pensions like Old Age Security, the Guaranteed Income Supplement and the Canada Pension Plan? Would they have cut other social expenditures?
I remember that when we brought in the six and five program, the Opposition did not support us. They claimed that it was unfair to make the cuts or impose the restraints, yet now they tell us that they would have reduced the deficit dramatically.
That does not wash, Mr. Speaker. Would they have cut defence expenditures? Would they have cut economic development expenditures during a recession when industry was on its knees and needed the assistance the federal Government could provide? Would that Party have cut job creation? I know it did in 1979 when it came to power. But during the middle of a recession when jobs were being lost by the thousands, would that Party have cut federal assistance for job creation? I do not think so, Mr. Speaker. Faced with the reality of power, of being the managers in a time of serious economic recession, I do not believe that any responsible Party would have made

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Evans
those kinds of moves, which would have led to a much larger deficit than the one we are seeing right now. I certainly hope no Party in this Canadian federal scene would have done that.
However, the question does come up as to what that Party would have done differently, and what would it do that is different from what we are doing? I believe the people of Canada are starting to ask that question more and more. They are not very happy with the answer which keeps coming back because, Mr. Speaker, of what we are hearing. The Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) told us last year that if he were faced with the same situation as the Minister of Finance, he would do basically the same thing. Yet here in the House he says, "We would reduce that deficit." That was all he talked about during his whole criticism-ninety minutes on the deficit.
What about the future? The Hon. Member for St. John's West has told us a great deal. First, a few months ago he was asked what the Conservative Party would do. He said in essence, "If I told you, we would never be elected". In other words, if the Conservatives told the people of Canada what they would do, they would never be elected. And, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for St. John's West did it again last night. I quote the following from the Ottawa Citizen of February 16:
Mulroney said the $31.5-billion deficit indicates the Liberal government is on the verge of bankruptcy and what Canadians really need is a new government.
However, Tory finance critic John Crosbie conceded that the government action needed to slash the deficit would scare most Canadians.
The article goes on to say:
"You have to be mean, nasty and do all sorts of unpleasant things," Crosbie said outside the Commons when asked what a Conservative government would do. "That's why I'm not going to outline what they would be now."
In other words, the Tories have a little plan. I mentioned in this House before that these Tories have a little list. They admit to a list of 3,500 names of individuals in the bureaucracy whom they are going to sack, so to speak, and I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that that list is probably a lot longer. Not only do they have a little list, they have a little plan, and that little plan, to quote the Hon. Member for St. John's West, would be, "mean, nasty and do all sorts of unpleasant things". That is the little plan, Mr. Speaker. I believe all we have to do is to go through the expenditures put forward in the Budget, the expenditure envelopes, and we would find out what that little plan entails. We have heard a few things which the Opposition Members said they would do. They would increase defence spending. They would increase transfers to the provinces for medicare. They would reduce taxes, which would reduce revenues, of course.
If one looks through the economic envelopes, Mr. Speaker, what are the Government's expenditures? Next year, $11.2 billion will be expended by this federal Government for economic development; $4 billion for energy development, new energy resources; $2 billion for legal affairs and justice in the country; $4.2 billion for servicing of roads and harbours and all of the things which come under the rubric of service to Government, buildings, national monuments, national parks,
all these things which are the responsibility of the federal Government in the form of infrastructure. There will be $192 million for Parliament. If you eliminated Parliament, it would not get you very much. On defence, $8.7 billion, will be expended. External Affairs and aid, $2.7 billion. Would there be a cut in external affairs and aid? Fiscal arrangements, $5.9 billion, that is equalization. I do not believe a Conservative Government would cut equalization to the provinces, but perhaps it would. Public debt charges, $20.4 billion. All of those areas, Mr. Speaker, could possibly be reduced by a government which was intending to be "mean, nasty and do all sorts of unpleasant things". The big one, however, in here, Mr. Speaker, is Social Affairs, $39.7 billion. I have the little thought in my mind, Mr. Speaker, and other Hon. Members are beginning to come to the same conclusion, that that is where the little plan is to be found, in the social affairs envelope. If the deficit is going to be reduced, social affairs is what that Party would go after. We proved, Mr. Speaker, during the recession, and we are proving in the Budget which came down, that that is not something which this Government will do. This Government will fight against reducing the money for social affairs.
We have heard a great deal about the deficit. I quote from the Montreal Gazette of February 16 where the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) is quoted as saying:
"There's nothing in this budget that deals with the fundamentals, namely an overwhelming deficit that is going to inhibit economic recovery," Mulroney told reports.
The Tory leader said there was "a degree of profligancy in government spending that is without precedent in any western industrialized nation."
Those are direct quotes from the Leader of the Opposition last night. Let us take a good look at this deficit, Mr. Speaker, a good hard look, because the fear is being put into the minds and hearts of Canadians that this deficit is going to destroy the nation, that it is going to bring us down. If we take the deficit in perspective, it seems to me, and I believe to most Canadians, that there used to be a time-and I suppose 1 show my age by remembering that time-when you could buy an automobile for $2,500. In fact, if I go back to my very early years, I can remember the days when you could buy an automobile for about $1,200. Today it costs $12,000. A person who bought a $1,200 car perhaps had to borrow $800. A person who buys a $12,000 car today might have to borrow $10,000 or $11,000. That is a huge increase in the notion of debt. However, at the same time incomes have gone up, Mr. Speaker. People can afford to service a larger debt. It seems to me that the notion of income, how rich we are, should have some bearing on how much debt we can afford to carry.
Let us look at the net public debt-that is the figure of which the Hon. Member for St. John's West was talking-as it relates to total personal income, the income of all Canadians in the country. In the 1983-84 period when we hit the worst of the recession, that ratio was 45.1 per cent. In other words, net public debt was 45 per cent of total personal income. That is the entire debt, not the deficit. The deficit is what you run up in one year. The debt is the cumulative total of all the previous deficits in history. That is a big number, 45 per cent, because
February 16, 1984

in the period from 1971 to 1982, the ratio ranged between 19 per cent and 33 per cent, basically. Now it is up to 45 per cent, and that is because of the big recession and the run-up of the current years' deficit and the effect it has had.
Let us go back historically, Mr. Speaker. This is supposed to be, according to the Leader of the Opposition, the worst situation which has ever existed. In 1946-47, the net public debt as a percentage of personal income was 132 per cent. In other words, the debt was a third larger than the total personal income. We should look through the period of time which we could call the Conservative halcyon days. I am talking about the time of the Diefenbaker Government, the period from 1957 to 1963. Let us look at the net public debt as a percentage of personal income during these halcyon days of conservatism when wealth and jobs were being created. We all agree the country was booming. We all agree the 1960s was a boom period for Canada. What were those figures? Remember, Mr. Speaker, that this year it is 45 per cent. Well, I'll be darned. In 1957-58 the ratio was 48.7 per cent; in 1958-59 it was 49.5 per cent; then 48.6 per cent, 47.2 per cent, 49.1 per cent, 47.3 per cent, and 47.8 per cent. This was all during the Diefenbaker period, the halcyon days of the Conservatives. The ratio of net public debt to personal income was higher during that entire period than it is right now when we are coming out of the worst recession the western world has known in the last 50 years. Those were the halcyon days. We were making great strides in personal income. But what happened to the debt, Mr. Speaker? Amazing, is it not? All during the 1960s the net public debt as a percentage of personal income was higher for every year than it is right now. The Hon. Member for St. John's West rails at the Government: "Oh, my gosh, we are going down the sewer". Well, we did not go down the sewer in the 1960s. The country did quite nicely.
I suggest the reason this net debt position is where it is right now is that this Government took the action necessary to protect Canadians during the worst recession we have seen in 50 years. Can you imagine what would have happened to Canadians, what it would have been like in this country over the last year and a half, or what it would be like right now if we had not taken the action we have? There would be chaos in the streets, Mr. Speaker. This Government supported the social programs it put in place over the years, and we continue to do so in this Budget.
We are now making structural changes to those programs to improve pensions, improve the environment for small business, because we believe that is where the jobs will be created in the future. We are making it easier for people to form and run small businesses and be successful. That will generate the jobs, Mr. Speaker, and this Budget moved very strongly in that direction. It is going to reduce the tax statutes applying to small business by two thirds. If you have three inches of tax statutes now, you are going to wind up, with these measures in place, with one inch.

speechtext:
I will believe it when I see it.
The Budget-Mr. Evans
