I think we should probably get down to the point where they are a quarter of an inch. I and some of my colleagues on both sides will continue to work together to see if we cannot get it down to a quarter of an inch from three inches. That would certainly be a boon. The Minister of Finance has moved dramatically in that direction.
Let us look at another set of figures. The Leader of the Opposition has said that there is a degree of profligacy in Government spending without precedent in any western industrialized nation. What would that be, Mr. Speaker? Let us say federal expenditures as a percentage of the GNP are now 9.2 per cent.
May I have unanimous consent to have one more minute to complete my remarks, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent for the Hon. Member to extend his remarks?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would like to thank my colleagues, Mr. Speaker. I was saying that federal expenditures as a percentage of the GNP now are 9.2 per cent. In 1979, the year of the Conservative Government, the ratio was 13.8 per cent, or about 33 per cent higher than it is now. My gosh, if we go back to those halcyon Diefenbaker years, it was 10.1 per cent, 11.7 per cent, 9.3 per cent, 10 per cent. Higher than it is now, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me we had better take a look at facts before we start crying wolf, because there is a lot of information which has not been portrayed correctly by the Hon. Member for St. John's West. I certainly hope that in future speeches on this Budget those facts will have some impact on the kind of commentary we hear relating to this Budget.
I tell you, Mr. Speaker, the Budget is a responsible one given the conditions we face. It makes great strides in terribly important areas. I am proud to stand up on this side of the House and support that Budget to the hilt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member's eloquent words and how pleased he is with the Budget. I have two questions. He made many comments regarding the real job creation to occur in Canada. In the next number of years that will obviously come from the small and medium-sized business sector. Governments are not going to be creatings jobs, and I do not think that anyone believes the corporate sector will be creating the jobs. So we are moving from the megaproject approach down to the microproject approach in job creation.
I read some of the quoted remarks of Mr. Bulloch, President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, who had some observations on the Budget last night. He agreed there were many positive steps of a housekeeping nature for small business in the Budget. However, he said the Budget itself will not result in any new real job creation in the small business sector. In other words, the Budget is not going to encourage small business to expand and create jobs. There seems to be some opposition to what the Hon. Member was saying. Would

February 16, 1984
The Budget-Mr. Evans
the Hon. Member not consider it to be advantageous for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) to have rescinded the personal tax increases Canadians are going to experience this year as a result of the April Budget? These amount to something in the neighbourhood of $1.4 billion for this particular year. In a recovery which will be consumer led, or where consumers will play a major role, would it not have been useful to rescind that tax increase?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, it would not have been. If you want consumption, the best place to get 100 per cent consumption is exactly where we got it: we increased the GIS. They are the people in greatest need. They do not save any of it, they spend it all. That is hundreds of millions of dollars being put in the hands of people who are going to spend it. That was where it should have been put, and that is where we put it.
As to Mr. Bulloch, I have great respect for him. I do not think there are many people who understand the small business environment better than he does. However, I suggest that by removing the cumulative deduction account, businesses will now be encouraged to expand. They have been afraid to do so because once they go beyond the $1 million limit, they are no longer a small business and the tax implications are horrendous. Therefore, we are removing the CDA and saying, $200,000 a year without limit. Businesses will feel unshackled. They are going to be free to expand, and I think they will.
The other thing this Budget did, and I think commentators across the land have been saying this, is to provide a sense of stability. The Minister of Finance did not make dramatic changes. He put in measures that were structural in nature and made the kind of changes which people are going to appreciate in the area of pensions, mortgages, and small business taxation. It came out as a Budget which maintains the sense of stability and purposefulness which the Government has put forward in the past. That is going to increase business confidence and, with the restraint measure, it will keep Government price increases down to the 4 per cent level. That reinforces the sense that we are going to get inflation under control. Those are the kinds of things we have to do if the confidence is going to be there for the real interest rate to start to squeeze down. When people no longer believe that inflation is going to take off again, interest rates will begin to come down closer to the inflation rate. That is what we need to do. That is built on stability, confidence and sound budgetary management, which is exactly what the Minister brought forward here last night.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed the comments of my colleagues. He pointed out the constructive role that government spending can play in softening the effects of economic slowdowns and recessions, particularly the effects that government spending can have on low income people. He also pointed out the Conservative policy to be "nasty, mean-minded and tough". I would like to quote something from the Toronto Star of February 12 which goes one step further than that. Joseph
Schlesinger, an impartial man who is a foreign correspondent for the CBC, has written the following:
Canada and the United States have both been going through tough times the past three years with high unemployment, increasing poverty and strained budgets.
But there is a major difference in how the two countries have dealt with the victims of the hard times.
Call it the Compassion Difference. But they try-
That is the Government of Canada:
-with job creation and income supplement programs. In the United States, the federal government is led by people who are not only cutting back on such help-they're actually denying the existence of some of the problems.
Edwin Meese, one of the President's closest political advisers, said:
-people go to soup kitchens because the food is free and that's easier than paying for it.
That is the Conservative mentality. In the House we have heard the Tory policy about being mean-minded and tough. That is what they are talking about. The Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said in the House that the Americans have handled the deficit properly. That is what he means. He has this cynical idea about poor people. The difference is the compassion difference. I would like to hear the Hon. Member's theories on that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is quite simple. It would have to be in order to get an answer from the other side. What am I now supposed to tell the more than 100,000 people who no longer qualify for unemployment insurance benefits
February 16, 1984

and do not qualify for welfare payments because they have a spouse working who earns just enough to keep them from qualifying? What do I tell those people is in this Budget that will be of some assistance to them on Monday next? What can I suggest they should do in order to meet their mortgage commmitments and find a job in an area in Hamilton where 50 per cent of construction workers and 20 per cent of steel workers are out of work? We have had six plants close down in the last 14 months. There is a negative job growth. In other words, there are fewer jobs being created than there are people looking for them. What can I say to them? I have raised this question with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts). Although no doubt they both bleed quite honestly for those individuals, there is no one offering them any kind of assistance or help. What do I tell them about this Budget, given that the Government is able to find 190 million tax dollars to give to the oil companies? The Government is willing to forgo hundreds of millions of tax dollars in RRSP investments to those who already have enough. The Government is prepared to reduce the tax burden on lawyers, doctors and accountants. There is not one single item in the Budget that I can find which addresses their immediate needs.

There is hope for those people with whom we all suffer. There is hope. The Government is putting in place policies which are going to do the absolute maximum that can be done in the situation which we face as a nation.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of minutes. I will make a few comments and call it six o'clock, if I may. The Hon. Member talks about the fantastic initiatives of the Minister of Transport. They should take the Minister of Transport, put him in a caboose and send him across the
Adjournment Debate
Prairies on a train. He would learn something about the railroad business. I say that because he was part of the Cabinet committee that allowed the dismantling of VIA Rail. At the time they said they were going to save $100 million. The Hon. Members opposite are making pious Alice in Wonderland comments and statements. I have never heard such a bunch of nonsense in my life. In 1981-82, VIA Rail cost $540 million. The Minister of Transport was going to save $100 million. That meant that the deficit should have gone down with regard to VIA. This year it costs $825 million. He cut off the revenue base and kept the cost structure the same. That is the fantastic initiative that the Minister of Transport is presiding over. They are all mad hatters. I get so excited that I cannot even talk. On February 1, 1983, they talked about 375,000 jobs that this rail initiative would create in western Canada. That was from the former Minister of Transport.

subtopic: HOUSING-RESIDENTIAL REHABILITATION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR EXPANSION. (B) DISTRIBUTION OF FUNDING
HOUSING-RESIDENTIAL REHABILITATION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR EXPANSION. (B) DISTRIBUTION OF FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 10 I raised a question with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) concerning RRAP, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. At the time I pointed out that this was a good program but limited to designated communities and neighbourhoods, which meant that many Canadian people were unable to take advantage of it.
Let me summarize some of the values of the RRAP program. First, it meets a real need for up-grading homes. It helps people, many of them on fixed incomes, to fix their places of residence. This is also available for rental units.
Second, it has an immediate and direct impact upon employment. The RRAP program is labour intensive.
Third, there are direct spin-offs to local communities. When people fix up their homes they are purchasing building materials and supplies at local stores. The RRAP program gets money to people who need to repair their homes and it creates

February 16, 1984
Adjournment Debate
jobs. However, as I said, the major problem with it is that it has never been adequately funded.
There are hundreds of communities and neighbourhoods across Canada that are left out of this program. There are three communities in my riding that have never been designated. Many of these people live close to rural areas where their neighbours have access to the RRAP program. They can see some of their neighbours across the road who have access to RRAP, only to find out when they apply that they are not eligible. Many of them live in older homes that are badly in need of renovation. Pensioners who live on fixed incomes see their neighbours across the road who are able to take advantage of the program. They make inquiries only to find that they are ineligible because their community has never been designated. The unfairness of this should disturb us all.
In the case of one municipality, I have been writing to the Minister and CMHC since 1980 in an attempt to get some action to have that community designated as being eligible for the RRAP program. In April, 1981, I was assured that the community of North Cowichan was on the priority list but the new funds had to be allocated. However, in December, 1982, during which time the economy of North Cowichan had declined considerably and the need was even greater, the Minister wrote that the communities of North Cowichan, Duncan and Ladysmith were not considered priority areas.
In the correspondence I have received from the Minister about this issue, he continuously refers to the shortage of funds and budgetary restraints as the reason why these areas have not been designated.
One of the many disappointments of yesterday's Budget was that it did not expand this program which is acknowledged on all sides of the House to be a good one. It is a good program that would put money into the hands of home owners who would, in turn, pass it on to trades people and local business. It is the kind of pump primer we on this side of the House have been saying our economy needs. However, the Minister and the Government answer that budgetary restraints make it impossible to expand this program.
In yesterday's Budget, we saw how some of these budgetary restraints are applied to some other sectors of the economy. For example, oil companies received a gift of an extra SI90 million from the suspension of the incremental oil revenue tax until June 1, 1985. We heard the Minister of Finance talk about doubling and tripling the tax exempt ceilings on RRSPs. This is a proposal that will directly benefit the well-to-do. As we all know, low and middle income people are unable to put aside the present $5,500 maximum tax exemption for an RRSP for a year, let alone the $10,000 limit for 1985 or the $15,000 limit for 1988. This increase in RRSP tax exemptions is a tax break for the well-do-do which will amount to $675 million in the next few years.
It is not as though we need to have more money put into savings. We have seen massive bail-outs for large corporations. In the last two weeks we have heard of a $150 million Liberal
slush fund. If the Government forgot about this business of using public money to curry favour with special constituencies and concentrated on getting Canadians the best value for their money, perhaps our economy would not be in such a mess.
Communities across Canada have been waiting for RRAP designation for years. They have been standing at the end of a long line which never seems to move. I call upon the Government to take some action to expand this program and to put money into it so that we can fix up our homes, create employment and get the economy moving again.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Claude Malepart (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: HOUSING-RESIDENTIAL REHABILITATION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR EXPANSION. (B) DISTRIBUTION OF FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to answer the questions raised by the Hon. Member for Cowi-chan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) on February 10, 1984 concerning the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, RRAP for short.
As the Hon. Member pointed out, RRAP has been an outstanding success. Since it was launched in 1974, some 262,000 housing units have been rehabilitated throughout Canada. In the past two years, the Federal Government has allocated $359 million to finance the program, including $309 million subject to repayment. Thanks to that assistance, approximately 89,000 units have been rehabilitated. Twice in 1983, additional funds were set aside for RRAP. For instance, the April budget earmarked $40 million for that program over a two-year period. An additional amount of $40 million was allocated in October so that the program would continue uninterrupted until the end of the year. Those measures are a clear indication of the Federal Government's commitment to maintain the quality of existing housing units. We will continue to support the program in 1984 because it has been widely accepted by Canadians and we want as many people as possible to benefit from it.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that many regions in this country have already been designated as eligible for RRAP. Although the Federal Government acknowledges that the Program is not offered in all regions, except in the case of handicapped persons, one of the Program's objectives is to promote upgrading of communities and consequently, the Program concentrates on areas where housing conditions are poor. Eligibility for the Program has had to be restricted because of high demand and a limited budget.
As the Minister indicated in his answer in the House, it would be unfair to make the Program's application universal without increasing funding, since people who already applied some time ago might be deprived of assistance under the Program.
I appreciate the Hon. Member's interest in RRAP and his support for the Program. Federal housing programs are constantly being reassessed in order to improve them. RRAP is being reviewed, and special consideration is being given to the feasibility of extending eligibility to Canadians in all regions.
February 16, 1984

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-DENIAL OF DEDUCTION FOR LEG BRACES. (B) REQUEST FOR BROADER DEFINITION OF "DISABILITY"
NATIONAL REVENUE-DENIAL OF DEDUCTION FOR LEG BRACES. (B) REQUEST FOR BROADER DEFINITION OF "DISABILITY"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 16 1 put a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) regarding a constituent of mine, Mr. David Bourne, who, as I said in the question, has felt the sting of the Income Tax Act in that he is being denied a deduction for expenses related to the cost of leg braces and is being told by National Revenue officials that he should use a wheelchair. I have protested to the Minister about this. I have asked him to review the statute and the regulations to see whether or not some adjustment could be made. There was a case before the tax court of a Mr. Michael Overdyk who has a disability similar to that of Mr. Bourne. The Tax Review Board ruled in favour of Mr. Oberdyk. I asked the Minister to look into this to see whether this could be a precedent applied to other people in the same condition.
The difficulty is this. My constituent is a young man. He is able to get around with leg braces and crutches. He is able to take employment. In fact, he was working for BP Petroleum which eventually became PetroCan. With braces and crutches, he was able to walk and get around his office. He is mobile in a car. He can go for a walk, walk his dog and so forth. If he goes into a wheelchair, there is a psychological problem that I will explain in a moment. In a wheelchair, he would have great difficulty in securing employment and carrying out the normal functions of life.
Many small employers have their offices on the second floor of buildings and in many cases there is no elevator. The doorways may not be wide enough and the washrooms may not be able to accommodate a wheelchair. The man is mobile, but the psychological impact of going into a wheelchair would be disastrous.
I personally know this because I was crippled with polio. For four years as a boy I used braces and crutches. I was pulled around on a wagon by my friends. I know how these braces have to be made and adjusted every year, sometimes twice a year. I was growing. I know when I fell down how they would hurt. I was bruised and skinned from the damned things. I was one of the lucky ones who was able to recover.
I know what this man is going through. He desperately wants to maintain the use of these leg braces, which cost more than a wheelchair. Every year he has to have them adjusted and renewed. This man wants to retain the use of them as long as he possibly can. He is part of the whole like everybody else in the office. He can get around, get out in case of fire and drive his car. He is just like everyone else, except he is a little slower. If you put him in a wheelchair, he will feel restricted.
I ask the Minister to look into the matter on humanitarian grounds. I have written to him about it, raised the matter in the House and have spoken to him privately. I cannot understand why the department does not move.
Adjournment Debate
There is a similar case in Hamilton. Professor Nagler who teaches at Waterloo University has cerebral palsy. He can drive a car, dress himself and do many of the everyday functions, but he cannot hold a pen or pencil in his hand and he cannot operate a typewriter. In order to perform his function as a teacher in a university he has to hire a secretary. The university does not provide that service for him. In order to perform any teaching function he has to hire a secretary to whom he dictates his notes. In that way he carries out his function as a teacher. He is a useful, intelligent individual. I cannot understand why the Income Tax Act cannot be amended to accommodate these people.
In my supplementary question to the Minister I asked why the Government did not accept the recommendation made by the special committee of this House. The committee's resolution No. 46 would cover cases like David Bourne and Professor Nagler. If the Government accepted that recommendation these people would be accommodated and looked after. It is deplorable that the Government cannot move to look after these people, and let them be part of the mainstream of society.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-DENIAL OF DEDUCTION FOR LEG BRACES. (B) REQUEST FOR BROADER DEFINITION OF "DISABILITY"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding to give an answer, I have to remind the Hon. Member that I may not give any information with regard to the affairs of a particular taxpayer, including the taxpayer of which the original question made mention. I can deal with the generalities of the subject only. Also, although the Hon. Member in his original question referred to a denial of a deduction for leg braces, it is evident from his reference to a certain case that he really meant the denial of the disability deduction.
The law here is quite precise. The Hon. Member may not like the law and think it should read differently, but, if that is the case, his quarrel should not be with the department which is required to administer the law as it is. The law says, in the context that concerns us here, that the disability deduction is available to a person who is:
-throughout a 12-month period ending in the year, necessarily confined for a substantial period of time each day ... to a bed or wheel chair-
The law, therefore, defines disability in terms of confinement to a bed or wheel chair, and that is the law to be administered.
In the Overdyk case, which is public knowledge the Tax Review Board, now the Tax Court, dealt with a particular set of facts. I may say that other cases where the facts are the same would be dealt with by the department according to the decision in the Overdyk case.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO VANCOUVER OFFICE PRACTICES. (B) JOB DESCRIPTION REFERENCE TO WORK QUOTAS
NATIONAL REVENUE-REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO VANCOUVER OFFICE PRACTICES. (B) JOB DESCRIPTION REFERENCE TO WORK QUOTAS
speechtext:
I am pleased to rise this evening to pursue a question I asked in this House earlier this

February 16, 1984
Adjournment Debate
week concerning the imposition of quotas on Revenue Canada taxation offices, particularly in the Vancouver regional office of Revenue Canada Taxation.
Since I first raised this issue of quotas and the deletion of reference to quotas in the Vancouver office early last week, I have been flooded with telephone calls and correspondence from constituents, in Burnaby in particular, but also from people throughout the mainland, expressing their concern about the effects this kind of imposition of quotas has on the manner in which Revenue Canada goes about its business.
I should emphasize that certainly no one objects to performance standards, that is, to standards that reasonably attempt to set out criteria that must be met by employees of Revenue Canada in pursuing their responsibilities. Similarly, no one takes objection to the suggestion that those taxpayers who are able to pay their tax and are deliberately avoiding payment of taxation should, in fact, be vigorously pursued. But in these difficult economic times surely it is not reasonable that Revenue Canada's authorities-the taxation authorities-should be cracking down, if you will, on the victims of this Government's economic policies; at a time when there are far too many people out of work and at a time when small businesses are really under the impact of this Government's economic policies. Surely Revenue Canada should not be operating under a system that forces staff to adhere to what amounts to quotas.
In making these comments I am not seeking to punish those who are the staff members of Revenue Canada. I think it is important the public be aware that these policies are policies which are developed by the Government, by senior staff members in national headquarters, by management, and in many instances the staff are simply administering these policies.
For example, it was not employees of the taxation component Department who made the decision to store all taxpayer files in Canada in seven central locations. It was not decided by employees of the Department that there should be quotas. Similarly, it was not employees who decided that taxpayer phone calls to Revenue Canada offices should be limited to three minutes each.
But for the director of the Vancouver office of Revenue Canada Taxation to deny the existence of quotas flies in the face of all of the evidence. In fact, senior staff in the Vancouver office of Revenue Canada Taxation went to such lengths to deny the evidence of quotas that they literally took a bottle of typewriter white-out fluid and blanked out all references to quotas on documents within the Vancouver office. There were a few documents they were not able to white-out. One was the actual job description for a PM3, Collections Unit Head.
That job description, which is in effect throughout Canada, states that one of the requirements of this particular individual is to:
-observing fluctuations in workload and production and establishing work quotas for each function-
How on earth can the Minister continue to deny the existence of quotas in Revenue Canada taxation offices when the very job description for a unit head in a Revenue Canada taxation
office clearly states that one of the obligations is to ensure that these quotas are met. We are getting some sort of doublethink or doublespeak. When the Minister continues to deny the existence of these quotas. We are not talking about the auditing function, we are talking about collections.
The implications of these quotas for taxpayers are clear. Far too many taxpayers are being unduly harassed. Their wages are being garnisheed in order that a staff member in question might meet a quota. Liens are being slapped on property, and telephone calls are being cut short. In essence, the high standard of service, which I am sure employees would like to be in a position to deliver to taxpayers, is suffering.
I should like to state very clearly that I believe that those of my constituents in Burnaby, who in many instances have been unduly harassed as a result of the policy of imposition of quotas, demand first of all a recognition of the existence of these quotas and, second and more important, an end to quotas.
Surely employees of Revenue Canada can go about their responsibilities in a manner that does not involve meeting a specific number of accounts per given period of time. Surely it is unacceptable that senior staff of the Vancouver office of Taxation Canada should deliberately set out to destroy evidence of quotas. That kind of conduct is unacceptable in the Public Service. The Regional Director of Taxation Canada must accept the responsibility for that totally inappropriate conduct.
There must be a full, independent inquiry into what led to his initial denial and subsequent cover-up of the existence of these quotas.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO VANCOUVER OFFICE PRACTICES. (B) JOB DESCRIPTION REFERENCE TO WORK QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) has answeered again and again in this House the allegations about auditors' quotas. He has done so with what I can only term exemplary patience. I will, therefore, not bother to cover the same ground.
The Hon. Member is talking about forms used in one office of the Department which refer to the expected or actual production of collection officers, not auditors. The Minister has never said that production standards are not set in the Department. In fact, a primary aim of the Department is to make the best, most efficient use of all its resources, material and human. It has a system of allocating these resources between functions and between offices in a way that is intended to optimize productivity. Expected production in each type of operation is highly important in this allocation process.
The Member should be aware that even the Auditor General has approved the approach of setting performance indicators for employees in the Government and that this is just a good management practice.
The Hon. Member has come into possession, by whatever means, of an internal operating document of the district office concerned. Through some local confusion of a junior supervi-
February 16, 1984

sor that document was changed. The Hon. Member seems to find something sinister here that escapes me. Surely anyone wishing to "cover up" something, with any improper intent- the Hon. Member used the words "cover up the evidence" in his original question-would not be so naive and literal as to use one of the patented white liquid correction fluids. To be very simpleminded about it, as the Hon. Member may not know but should, the fluid leaves a white smear that makes the
Adjournment Debate
correction glaringly obvious. There are many ways to change a record when you have something to hide, but this must be the worst of all ways.
